speechtext: House resumed the adjourned debate on the proposed motion of Mr. Borden for the second reading of Bill (No. 115), to provide for the extension of the boundaries of the province of Manitoba.

Mr. Speaker, the question which is now before the House is one of great importance indeed and of far-reaching consequences from the national point of view, and, I might perhaps add, from the imperial point of view. We are engaged in the process of carving out from the vast domain of Rupert's Land new territories for three great provinces of this Dominion. Whilst we are engaged in thus carving out these new territories we might, perhaps, be inclined to forget the men who secured for Canada the great Rupert's Land, obtaining it through the good offices of Downing street for a paltry sum of money. I have heard during this debate warm compliments paid to the memory of Sir John
A. Macdonald, who was declared to be a great statesman because, in the early days of confederation, he had thought proper to enter into negotiations with the mother country in order to secure these territories for the Dominion of Canada. I do not begrudge, Sir, the compliments to which the great giant of our Canadian public life, Sir John A. Macdonald, is entitled. But, we must not forget, now that we are comparatively far away from those events of confederation days, that there were other men too who did their best to obtain the union of the various provinces and to found this great confederacy, and who, with Sir John Macdonald, merged their party strife and party spirit and obtained for Canada the territories of the northwest from the Hud1-son's Bay Company. 1 refer especially to the ,old Liberal chieftain, George Brown and Alexander Mackenzie, to whom we owe much for confederation and for the retention of this land for the Dominion.
With this piece of legislation which we are now considering stands on the order paper concurrent legislation, which will be moved in a few days by my right hon. friend who leads the government (Mr. Borden). There are two resolutions on the order paper in one of which it is enacted that what remains of the territory north of Ontario, and the portion of Keewatin that is not allotted to Manitoba, shall go to the province of Ontario. In another resolution it is also enacted that the far away district of Ungava, shall henceforth belong to the province of Quebec. Sir, let me say at once to my right hon. friend the Prime Minister that, speaking as a Canadian, I heartily approve of that legislation. I believe that Ontario is entitled to the land north of Temiskaming as far as the shores of Hudson bay and I unreservedly, rely on the good sense of the province of Ontario to administer that new region as well as it has administered the district immediately adjoining. I also approve of the annexation of Ungava to the province of Quebec. It rightfully belongs to the province of Quebec. My hon. friends, the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier), and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Monk), yesterday, opened their remarks by laying emphasis on the fact that Ungava would be allotted to the province of Quebec. Presumably they were desirous of accommodating their remarks as much as they could, to the sentiments of their followers in this House. But their followers and the members of this House must not forget that both the territory to the north of Ontario and Ungava territory were offered some years ago by a Liberal government to the two largest provinces of the Dominion. Ontario did not see fit at the time to accept the terms of the 'resolution which was moved in this House by my right hon. friend who leads

the opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), but long ago, Quebec, through the instrumentality of the Premier, Sir Lomer Gouin, accepted Ungava on behalf of his /province. So, it is no. new thing and Ungava cannot suffice to soothe the sentiments of the followers of hon. gentlemen opposite. They must give something else. At all events, Sir, I congratulate the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden) not on having given these portions of the northern territories to the two great provinces of Ontario and Quebec, but rather do I congratulate him upon having only implemented legislation brought before this House three or four years ago.
Let me say now, how far I disagree with the right hon. gentleman in regard to the legislation which he has submitted to this. House. There is another order in council which will toe embalmed in the statute book, I suppose, as part of the Bill. This order in council has reference to the projection of a line five miles in width through the northern territory of Manitoba as far as Port Nelson. I cannot help saying with all due respect to my right hon. friend, that this is a most unseemly and most extraordinary piece of legislation. It paves the way for future conflicts between the provinces of Manitoba and the province of Ontario. It gives sovereign rights to the province of Ontario on that thin red line on the map, whilst it keeps away from Manitoba proprietary Tights in the lands adjoining.
I say it paves the way for future conflicts between these two great provinces. True, the Prime Minister can answer that the Premier of Manitoba is satisfied, and that the Premier of Ontario, who is supposed to voice public opinion in that province, is equally satisfied, and that the government supporters at Ottawa are satisfied, and that the opposition in this House are the only persons who are dissatisfied.
Hear, hear.

Well, that is no argument. My right lion, friend the Prime Minister is supposed to know public opinion in this country and he ought to realise that he cannot repeat the victory he won on the wave of the 21st of September last. He may believe that, but, there was once a king of Poland who, when he was intoxicated, believed that all his subjects were intoxicated with him. And, as regards this unseemly projection of the province of Ontario in a thin red1 line on the map towards Port Nelson, I say with all due Te-spect for Sir James Whitney, for whom I have great admiration
Hear, hear.

I say that notwithstanding all his ability, while he may be satisfied with that thin red line projected over Manitoba to Port Nelson, there are others deeply interested in the province of Ontario who are not satisfied. I know of a man who in his day and generation represented public opinion in Ontario in no less degree than does Sir James Whitney; I refer to Sir Oliver Mowat.
Hear, hear.

I know the fight and the successful fight that Sir Oliver Mo^wat made for the boundaries of Ontario against Sir John A. Macdonald; and I know that if Sir James Whitney is satisfied with this, Sir Oliver Mowat would not be satisfied were he alive to-day.
May I ask a question ?
Order, sit down.
I just want to ask a question.
Take your medicine like a man.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) has the floor.
I am now in the vein of paying compliments to the Prime Minister and that stalwart friend of his, that future cabinet minister
Now, you have got him.

He should not interrupt me even ' pro bono publico.' I am, I say in the vein of paying compliments to the right hon. the Prime Minister, and coming to the boundaries of Manitoba I say that I approve of the boundaries as set forth in this Bill. I approve because it is a vindication of the policy pursued by Sir Wilfrid Laurier when he was in office. That right hon. gentleman himself mapped cut with his colleagues what extensions should be made to Manitoba north and east, but for years and years the Manitoba government who were not in sympathy with the right hon. gentleman, marked -time. They sent to Ottawa delegation after delegation, and when they were not satisfied with the boundaries they were satisfied with other parts of the offer made to them, but it was always found that if something was satisfactory something else) was sure to be unsatisfactory in the terms offered by the Liberal government. By far, the most important matter was the provision with regard to the boundaries, and it is a vindication of the policy of Sir Wilfrid Laurier that exactly the same boundaries have been given to Manitoba in this Bill as he proposed. And, if the present Prime Minister, in addition to extend-
MAltCH 6, 1912
ing the boundaries of Manitoba and giving new wheat fields to the farmers of that province, could insert in that Bill a provision that with respect to the new crops that will be raised on that extended territory he would give to the western farmer a market in which to sell them I would say that this legislation was almost perfect. Be that as it may, the Prime Minister did another thing by this legislation to which I strongly object.
I need not repeat the arguments that have been adduced by the hon. member for St. 3ohn (Mr. Pugsley). With his usual eloquence he dealt with this subject and he criticized with all the vigour and ability with which he is endowed the financial terms that are offered to Manitoba by this Bill. I agree entirely with the remarks he made. I say that the financial terms are exorbitant. I say that they are not what they should be, considering the position of Manitoba relative to the other provinces, and when we know that in 1885 there should have been a finality in this matter. The policy of the government as regards the arrears is also unsound and calculated1 .to bring about regrettable results. I agree on these two questions with my hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley). In giving "the enormous amounts which are being handed over to the province of Manitoba by this arrangement I cannot help thinking of the sad position in which the provinces by the sea are left. I cannot forget that the maritime provinces helped just as much as did Ontario and Quebec in the founding of this Dominion. I cannot help remembering that their delegates were united with the delegates of Ontario and Quebec, and that they thought when Canada was made a Dominion they would have an equal chance with the other provinces to develop and to increase. But what are the facts? As Quebec has increased her territory, as Ontario has increased her territory, as the provinces in the west are increasing their territory, the little provinces by the sea which cannot be extended are decreasing in population, while their financial burdens are ever increasing. Have not these provinces in the east done as much for confederation as have the new provinces? I have travelled in the west and I say here that the real pioneers are the men who came from the maritime provinces and from Quebec and from Ontario. You may go into any seat of learning in the west; you may go to any high school in these new territories, and there you will meet men from Prince Edward Island, men from Nova Scotia, men from New Brunswick, teaching the younger generation. Go into the banking institutions, into the insurance companies, into the largest financial establishments, and at the head of these institutions you will find men from the far away provinces by the sea, But,
Sir, the provinces by the sea will have no added territory. Then, under such circumstances, before carving out finally what remains of our Canadian Dominion, the right hon. gentleman should have summoned to Ottawa a conference of the premiers of the various provinces and have given our friends by the sea a chance to exist and to live. '
Mr. Speaker, the Bill is perhaps more important for what it does not contain than for what it contains. We were treated right royally last evening to the new issue of the eternally famous school question By whom has this question been imported into the debate? Not by the Liberal party, not by the Liberal press, not by the Liberal orators throughout the country. The question which was imported into the House last night must be assigned exclusively to the Nationalist wing of the coalition government. Indeed, I do not know why I should presently, address myself to my friends on the other side of the House. They know more about this feud than we " know. I ought to enlighten my friends on this side of the House who come from various provinces as to this family quarrel-because it is nothing more and nothing less than a family quarrel. My hon. friend the Postmaster General complained last night that he was being called names. He said:	' They call us names;
they implore us French Canadian ministers, hand over your portfolios; and we are branded as arch traitors.' Of course, Sir, the hon. gentlemen will not hand over their portfolios, and my hon. friend must stand being called names for many years to come. Turning towards his Tory friends sitting behind him, he said, "They call us arch traitors." By whom are they called arch traitors? As regards myself, I know what name to give the hon. gentleman. For twenty-five years in public life I need not invent any new name. He is called arch traitor by whom? By his own friends. Mr. Bourassa, in an interview published two days ago, said that the conduct of the hon. gentlemen who form the Nationalist wing of the coalition government made his British blood boil in his veins; and Mr. Ar-mand Lavergne, the leader of the hon the Postmaster General, said of him not later than yesterday, "I am ashamed of him." Arch traitors, Mr. Speaker? Arch traitors to their own friends, whom they led not into the promised land of integral Nationalism. Arch traitors to their own friends, to their own promises, and to their apparent convictions on and before the 21st of September last. I say again, Mr. Speaker, we did not raise the issue. We are simple onlookers. We are witnessingithe quarrel, and we are evincing much pleasure at the sight. No, we did not raise the issue. The best evidence of that is the able and eloquent speech delivered last night by a sincere

believer in Nationalism, the young member for Nicolet (Mr. Lamarehe) a speech Sir, which deserves commendation from every member of this House, because it was lofty. What did the hon. member for Nicolet say? He said that he felt in'duty bound to separate himself from his ministers who had led him astrav lefore Hie 21st of September, as he had promised if elected he would restore separate schools to Manitoba and would give separate schools to the minority in'-Keewatin. By whom was he induced to make that promise to the electors of the county of Nicolet if not by the Minister of Public Works, if not by the Postmaster General, and by the Minister of .Inland Revenue? I repeat-and I am in the judgment if my fellow Liberal members from the province of Quebec-who induced the bright young men who separated themselves yesterday from the ministerial party-who induced them during the last four years, in their respective constituencies, to advocate and promise the restoration of a system of separate schools in Manitoba and in the district of Keewatin, if not the Postmaster General the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Inland Revenue with their incendiary speeches? The quarrel is between those who yesterday separated themselves from the ministerial party and the three Quebec ministers is this, that the young Nationalists are sincere, while the three ministers are not and were not sincere. Sir, I have listened with a great deal of interest, with rapt attention, to the impetuous speech made by the Postmaster General. It was a plea pro domo.
The hon. gentleman was defending his own gates, he was defending his own lines, in a word he was defending his portfolio. But, Sir, do you suppose that this speech, hurling defiance as it did against the exPrime Minister, was addressed to the right hon. gentleman. Sir, the Postmaster General's bold rejoinder went far beyond the walls of this parliament: It was addressed to that Samson of the Nationalist party, that Samson that no Delilah could approach, and whose locks no Delilah can clip or fleece. The indignant speech of the hon. gentleman was addressed to Mr. Bourassa, who is now desecrating the ministerial temple by acting in such a way that we can already hear the columns toppling and tumbling to pieces within that edifice.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Hear, hear.

No, Mr. Speaker, that speech was not directed against the right hon. gentleman who leads the opposition, sure of that. The Postmaster General's indignant accents went far beyond the walls of this House. They were addressed against Mr. Bourassa, who dared to be logical after the 21st of September as he Mr. LEMIEUX.
was before that date. They were addressed against Mr. Lavergne, the would-be leader of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pelletier). They were addressed against the editors of the Nationalist press-against the editor of ' Le Devoir,' of ' La Croix,' of * Le Nationalists,' ' L'Action Sociale,' against the four leaders of public opinion in the Nationalist party, who are all denouncing the action of the Postmaster General at the present time. Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman and his colleagues from Quebec are primarily responsible for this school agitation and they will reap their reward sooner or later.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Hear, hear.

They are denounced by those they have misled. They will also be condemned by the electorate at the very first opportunity. Last night I heard something which is new to my ears. I listened to the laboured speech of the Minister of Public Works. I pinched myself during the delivery of that sp.eech. I could not believe that it was the Minister of Public Works who was speaking, but beyond doubt he was the speaker. He said, Mr. Speaker, that he always understood-and he made the statement in his usual mellifluous tones-that the school question had been finally settled, and he added, remembering no doubt that he once was a professor at Laval University, ' We are functi officio.' It sounded like a legal sermon. The Minister of Public Works during the last 15 years has been representing quite another constituency than that of Jacques Cartier; his constituency was the Nationalist element and some of the young clergy in the province of Quebec. I do not know what the Nationalists would have said during the last campaign, with the programme I have in my hand, when the hon. gentleman was apparently so much concerned about the maintenance of the federal pact of 1867 as regards the protection of all minorities in order to ensure contentment among all classes-if he had told them that the Manitoba school question had been settled.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Hear, hear.

I do not know either, what reception he would have had from a certain section of the Freneh-Canadian clergy if he had answered: * functi officio sumus ! ' Ah ! Mr. Speaker, we were great criminals in the province of Quebec. The right hon. gentleman who leads the opposition, with his Freneh-Canadian colleagues in the late cabinet, and the French Canadian members in the last parliament were great criminals in the eyes and in the judgment of the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Monk). True, at the same time whilst he was ingeniously

carrying on his racial agitation, by promising remedial legislation, by promising the restoration of Catholic schools in Manitoba, in Saskatchewan, and in Alberta, true it is that during his 15 years of stewardship in this parliament the hon. gentleman never moved a motion of censure against the settlement which was made in 1897. But one can speak one way before the House of Commons and the other way before the electorate; and we had the evidence of this during the last 15 years. Let me recall a few instances. Those whose righteous principles were elastic enough to accept the Manitoba settlement made by the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) in 1897 could perhaps be' stirred up in their patriotic feelings against the hon. gentleman's naval policy as formulated in this parliament, and, therefore, the Minister of Public Works made a formal alliance with the Nationalist party. With some of them he rode the separate school horse, with some others he rode with flying banners against the Canadian navy. And in order to give the public an impression that he was sincere, what did he do? He severed with eclat his connection with the right hon. gentleman who now leads the government.
He did that in order to give the Prime Minister a little more freedom elsewhere and to make himself a little more free in the constituencies of the province of Quebec. Many in this House were present in the county of Drummond and Arthabaska two years ago who have not forgotten the incident which took place during the speech of the hon. Minister of Public Works on that occasion. He was fiercely denouncing the naval law he was fiercely denouncing the school settlement promulgated at the instance of the right hon. gentleman by the Greenway government in Idanitoba, when suddenly, from the crowd, a voice shouted ' what about Borden?' My right hon. friend (Mr. Borden) will pardon me if I re-echo the very discourteous interjection, but great men are only known by their family names? Some one shouted from the multitude ' What about Borden?'
He is all right.
He is all right? He may be all right to-day
Hear, hear.

He may be all right today, but on that day he was all wrong. What was the answer of the Minister of Public Works? Let my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) a doughty fighter of the Conservative party, listen to this. When he was asked:	What about Borden?
he turned around and, nearly sobbing, as he sobs when he passes his estimates, with tears in his voice and in his eyes, said:
Borden? Have I severed my connection with the Conservative party to be told that I am a partisan of Borden? He was all wrong, Mr. Speaker, on that day.
I say, Sir, that the stand of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Monk) on the school question for the last 15 years,-and you, Sir, are a witness to this-was on a par with his stand on the naval question at the opening of this session. You remember, Mr. Speaker, in 1909, on the 29th March, a resolution was passed by this parliament praying for the establishment of a Canadian navy. You remern-bei that the hon. gentleman who is now Minister of Public Works, from his seat in this House, denounced that policy and declared himself opposed to that resolution. During the campaign his constituency of Nationalists listened to him. According to Mr. Bourassa and his friends he was the only one in this House who had spoken the true language of a patriot. The elections took place, and that hon. gentleman was selected as one of the colleagues of the Borden government. He came back-to this House, he was asked how the change had come about, what bargain he had made with the right hon. the Prime Minister, to merge his. opinions, anti-naval, with the opinions, pro-naval, of his Prime Minister. What did he answer? He answered that he had never wavered, that he had always been in favour of a naval policy. He went so far as to say that he had supported the resolution of Match 29, 1909, and I had to read him his ipsissima verba from the ' Hansard.' He did not dare answer when I established clearly to this House that he had differed completely from his colleagues on that occasion.
The Postmaster General made a lengthy speech containing some more or less witty references to the right hon. gentleman who-leads the opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), which, perhaps, could be forgiven, if they had been made on the platform or at Billingsgate, but I say that the reflections he cast on the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) will put the Postmaster General on a level where he really stands in the judgment of this House. Sir, let not my friends who belong to the Tory party believe for one moment, that this staunch defender of Tory faith, has always been a dyed-in-the-wool Tory. I know the hon. Postmaster General from A to Z, and when I say from A to Z, I know whereof I speak. The hon. gentleman reminds me of that little animal mentioned somewhere in the Roman law, known in common parlance as the chameleon, but known in the Roman law as the salamander. In the Roman.law a man who has a fraudulent debtor was called a salamander or a chameleon because he could change at his own sweet will. The

hon. gentleman is the Postmaster General, of Canada. Has he always been such a faithful follower of the Conservative party, has he always held the same contemptuous opinion which he expressed yesterday of the right hon. gentleman who leads the opposition? I tell niy hon. friends on your right, that I have known the Postmaster General for nearly 35 years. I have listened to him when he was a humble, a very humble follower of the right hon. gentleman who leads the opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). In 1885 on the Riel question, the hon. gentleman left the Tory party, joined the ranks of the Liberal party, and ran as the candidate of the Nationalist party of the time, in Three Rivers.
The Liberal-Nationalists.

The hon. gentleman who always refers to his loyalty and his sturdy opposition to reciprocity, was a humble follower of the right hon. gentleman who leads the opposition, when the Liberal party in 1891 unfurled the banner of unrestricted reciprocity. He supported that party from 1887 until 1891. In Lotbiniere county, in the elections of 1908, when he ran against my hon. friend who sits for Lotbiniere, he did not run as a Conservative candidate, he stood as an independent candidate. He wanted to come into this House-and I was present on the platform to unmask him he solicited the votes of the men of Lotbiniere county, as he said, that he might come into the House of Commons as a follower of the right hon. gentleman. Sir, during the last election, in the month of September he delivered a speech in the county of Quebec, where he was brought as a candidate ty whom? By Mr. Lavergne. Let me quote from * L'Evenement,' his own organ:
On the 17th of September, speaking dn the county of Quebec, Mr. Pelletier paid a tribute of gratitude to Messrs. Bourassa and Lavergne for what they had done for their country.
And in his grandiloquent style, with that tragic countenance which he assumed yesterday, reminding us of Talma or Coquelin, he said:
The people love you, Lavergne, because you have loved the people. Bourassa and yourself, Lavergne, have written a unique page in the annals of our country. I have offered myself as a candidate, because I had the support of Armand Lavergne.

And speaking of the multitude:

Do you think, Mr. Speaker, that Mr. Lavergne, on the 17th of September last, gave utterance to views similar to those that were expressed by his follower last night in this House? We all know as a matter of history, and you, Mr. Speaker, better than any one else, that the reason why Mr. Lavergne severed his connection from the Liberal party was, first, because on the Autonomy Bills of 1905, he deprecated the substitution of clause 16, No. 2, to clause 16 No. 1. Mr. Lavergne, in the province of Quebec-and I am in the judgment of the Liberal members of this House-Mr. Lavergne denounced the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier on the school question, and on the naval question. And when my hon. friend the Postmaster General ran as a candidate in Quebec county he ran imbued with the ideas, with the principles, with the professions of faith made by Mr. Lavergne; he was the follower of ,Mr. Lavergne, as he rightly stated at that meeting. What a change since the 21st of September. It may be said, however, Mr. Speaker, that not all of the Nationalist editors had faith in the hon. gentleman. My hon. friend has given a new version of the history of the Manitoba school question. Let me refer for a minute to this question which is better known probably from my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Rogers) than from any other member of the House of Commons. There was a school question from 1890 to 1897. but I understood last evening from the Minister of Public Works that it had been finally settled. The Postmaster 'General stated in so many words last evening that it was not settled and that he relied on his friend, Mr. Roblin, to give justice to the minority of Manitoba. It is well known that in 1890 a Grit government in Manitoba abolished the separate school system. It is also a matter of history that this legislation, passed by the Manitoba government in 1890, could have been disallowed within two years of its sanction. It was not disallowed, and I quite agree with my hon. friend that it would have been a very severe remedy to have
used against that legislation. Sir John Macdonald, we are told, refused to entertain the idea of disallowing that legislation in Manitoba. He had had his experience with that province of Manitoba; he knew that disallowance might be in the statute-book, but that it is never wise nor prudent for a statesman to enforce it. It was no more wise to use the power of disallowance than, in such an extreme position as the Manitoba school question was placed in 1896, to use the remedial order which was sent forward from the then government to the Manitoba authorities. If we cannot blame the Conservative government in 1890, 1891 and 1892 for not having used the power of disallowance, we cannot blame the Laurier government of 1896 for not having insisted on the remedial order being accepted by the Manitoba authorities, and I will explain why. The great mistake-I will not use the word ' crime,' because according to Thiers an error in politics is sometimes worse than a crime- the great mistake made by the Conservative party in 1890 was, instead of boldly facing the issue and entering into negotiations with the Manitoba government, to dally with the question, to send it from court to court, from the Supreme Court of 'Manitoba to the 'Supreme Court at Ottawa, from the Supreme Court at Ottawa to the Privy Council in England, from there again back to Manitoba, and to follow in the same way a second time to the Privy Council in London. During that time the agitation went on, becoming fiercer and fiercer every day, until, in 1895, this country, as you know, Mr. Speaker, being a contemporary yourself of the events which took place during those memorable years,
1895	and 1896, was ripe for civil war and we were, practically speaking, on the verge of national disintegration. What happened then? The judgment of the Privy Council came to the Conservative government and they enacted the famous remedial order. Looking back at those events as they appear in history to-day, is there a man in this House who. in his sober senses and in good faith, would pretend for one minute that the remedial order could have been enforced as against an unwilling legislature in Manitoba? I assert that it was impossible. Sir Charles Tupper, during the session of 1896, after the Liberal government came into office, admitted that it was impossible to enforce that remedial order. There is a saying in law-and again I address myself to an old, professor of constitutional law who will pardon me if I use Latin w-ords-summum jus summa injuria. We know that under the saving clause of the Manitoba Act you could enact remedial legislation, but by enforcing that legislation against an unwilling legislature in

Do you not rather believe, Mr. Speaker, you who are one of the stalwarts of the old Conservative party of those days, that the crisis which took place in the cabinet in 1895 -and 1896, when seven ministers on the eve of a session and of -a general eleotion, threw up their portfolios and abandoned their leader, reacted in the country and had the effect of opening the minds and -judgment of the electors? fellow citizens, and I know that if the time -comes when there are several French Canadian members in these two legislatures, as very likely it will, then the English speaking people of the western provinces will be generous enough to give them the opportunity of using their own language in addressing the legislative chamber. Well, there are just two or three words in the last sentence of the Quebec speech which do not sound like the usual utterances of the right hon. leader )f the oppoistion, and as to the balance of both speeches, I recognize the expression of his well-known principles of justice of fair-play and freedom for all the people of Canada irrespective of race or creed. And, Sir, I declare here without fear of contradiction that whether in Ontario or in Quebec the right hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier has always advocated only one policy: a policy oi conciliation and mutual concession. But we do not lack authority other than newspaper reports which are not always accurate; we have here the book of books; we have here ' Hansard,' and in	' Hansard ' will be found the
policy enunciated by the Rt. Hon. gentleman, when leader of the opposition, sitting in the very seat he now occupies, vindicating Liberal principles against a Conservative majority from 1890"to 1897. The letter I refer to was written by Father Lacombe, and addressing the Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, he said:
I inform you with regret that the episcopacy like one man, united to the clergy, will rise to support those who -may have fallen to defend us. Please pardon my frankness which leads me -to speak thus. Though I am not your intimate friend, still I may say that we have been on good terms. Always I have deemed you a gentleman, a respectable citizen and a man well able to be at the head of a political party. May Divine Providence keep up your courage and your energy for the good of our common country. We do not ask you to vote for the government hut for the Bill which will render us our rights, which will be presented to the House in a few days. I consider, or

rather we all consider, that such an aot of courage, goodwill and sincerity on your part, and from those who follow your policy, will be greatly in the interests of your party especially in the general elections.
There the chance was offered to the right hon. gentleman that if he would support the remedial legislation he would in return receive the support of the Catholic clergy of the province of Quebec. And, we were told from the government benches yesterday that Sir Wilfrid Laurier had appealed to the religious prejudices of his fellow countrymen, in 1896. How dare any man make such a statement? We have ' Hansard ' here,' and we have the words spoken by the right hon. gentleman before the elections, spoken not in a little hall in the back concessions of Quebec, nor in the back concessions of Ontario, but here on the floor of this parliament, addressed to the country and conscious that his words would be unmistakably heard by the people at .large, and what did Sir Wilfrid Laurier answer to that invitation of Father La-combe? Mark his words:
Not many weeks ago I was told from high quarters in the church to which I belong, that unless I supported the school Bill which was then being prepared by the government and which we have now before us, I would incur the hostility of a great and powerful body. Sir, this is too grave a phase of this question for me to pass it by in silence. I have only this to say: even though I have threats held over me, coming, as I am told from high dignitaries -in the church to which I belong, no word of bitterness shall ever pass my lips as against that church. I respect it and I love it; but Sir, I am not of that school which has been long dominant in France and other countries of continental Europe, which refuses to ecclesiastics the privilege of having a voice in public affairs, No, I am a Liberal of the English school; I believe in that school which has all along claimed that it is the privilege of all subjects, whether high or low, whether rich or poor, whether ecclesiastic or layman, to participate in the administration of public affairs to discuss, to influence, to persuade, to convince; but which has always denied, even to the highest, the right to dictate even to the lowest.
Was that an appeal to the passions of his fellow countrymen? 'Listen to the right hon. gentleman further:
I am here representing not Roman Catholics alone but Protestants as well, and I must give an account of my stewardship to all classes. Here am I, a Roman Catholic of French extraction entrusted, with the confidence of the men who sit around me, with great and important duties in our constitutional system of government. I am here the acknowledged leader of a great party composed of Roman Catholics and Protestants as well, in which the Protestants must be in the majority as in every party.
Am I to be told-I, occupying such a position-that I am to be dictated* to as to the course I am to take in this House by reasons that can appeal to the consciences of my fellow-Catholio members, but which do not appeal as well to the consciences of my Protestant colleagues? No! so long as I have a seat in this House, so long as I occupy the position I do now, whenever it shall become my duty to take a stand upon any question whatever, that stand I will take, not from the point of view of Roman Catholicism, not from the point of view of Protestanism, but from a point of view which can appeal to the consciences of men, irrespective of their particular faith, upon grounds which can be occupied by all men who love justice, freedom and toleration.
That programme-because it is a programme-became the banner of the Liberal party, French and English; it became the bond of union of all liberty-loving Canadians. It defeated the Tory policy, a policy which in Ontario vociferously denounced the right hon. gentleman for certain reasons, which I need not give, and which in Quebec, denounced him no less vociferously, and perhaps much more ingeniously, from quite other motives. The government of the day resigned, and as a result the right hon. gentleman, then became the Premier of this Dominion. He was immediately called upon to formulate a policy on the school question. Of course we hear much less denunciation against the Postmaster General and the Minister of Public Works than were made in 1896 against the right hon. gentleman. He had to give justice immediately to the Catholic minority of Manitoba, as the demand was pressing. It took a few months. He had some pour parlers with Mr. Greenway. He used the influence of his colleagues, Sir Oliver Mowat, and others, and finally an agreement was reached. The Minister of Public Works declared last night that that agreement was acceptable to him to-day. The question in his judgment, is finally settled. According to the Postmaster General, it was a poor settlement. Sir, the Postmaster General paid a great compliment to the memory of the old leader of the Liberal party, who has just passed away, the Hon. Edward Blake, and I join him in those compliments. If, according to my hon. friend, the Laurier-Greenway settlement was a poor one, one for which the right hon. gentleman should have been condemned 15 [DOT]years ago, how is it that Hon. Edward Blake, a great legal luminary probably the greatest jurist in the British Empire at any rate, strongly approved of that settlement? Edward Blake gave as his opinion that the settlement was a broad and fair settlement, and should be accepted by the minority in Manitoba; and we know that Mr. Blake

Then my hon. friend was good enough to lament the harsh treatment which, as he claims, has been meted out to the province of Ontario. Does he realize, when he makes that statement, that the boundaries proposed by this government are exactly the same as those for which he voted in 1908?
Does he realize that although Ontario, through her ministers of the Crown, went before the government of which he was a member, she was denied the relief which this government is giving her by the present measure? Now, Mr. Speaker, it must be apparent to you under those circumstances, that so far as these statutory provisions respecting separate schools in the northwest are concerned, they were absolutely inoperative, for the reason, in the first place, that no members of the Council had been appointed so as to create a body known as the Commissioner's Council, and in the next place, because the commission had not been authorized-even though councillors had been appointed-to make any laws or ordinances whatsoever with respect to the establishment of schools in these territories. The situation when we came into power was this: that for three years there had been upon the records of this parliament, resolutions declaring that the boundaries of Manitoba, of Ontario, and of Quebec, ought to be enlarged according to certain defined limits which were expressed in these resolutions. What was our duty under the circumstances ? We know very well indeed that a great deal of negotiation had gone on between the government of Manitoba and the late Liberal administration with regard to the enlargement of the boundaries of that province, and, there are those of us who are free to believe that the delays with respect to all these provinces were due to a certain peculiar policy of the Liberal government in connection with the extension of the boundaries of Manitoba. When we came to power, we conceived it to be our duty to carry out that policy which parliament had declared in 1908, and we proceeded to carry it out. I ask any hon. gentleman in this House whether or not it would have been a reasonable thing for this _ government-after that matter had stood for nearly four years without the appointment of any council, without authority to the commissioner to put into force these provisions respecting education- I ask whether or not it would have been a reasonable thing for us to undertake to do that without which these Northwest Territories had got on very well for three and-a-half years at least. And, to do that, remember, on the very eve of carrying out a proposal to which parliament had given its unanimous acceptance on the 13th of July, 1908. Why, Mr. Speaker, I think it would have been the verv worst thing we could have done in the interests of all concerned if this government had seen fit, on the eve of enlarging the boundaries of Manitoba, to take any such step as that which has been suggested. I come from a province where separate schools do not exist by reason of any statutory provisions; I come from the province of Nova Scotia, and I would like to tell my hon. friends in this House from the province of Quebec and from every other province in Canada, that although there are no provisions in that province establishing separate schools Mr. BOUDEN.
for Catholics as a matter of right, the relations between Protestants and Catholics in the province are, I believe, at least as cordial and as friendly as they are in any province of Canada, and I do not believe that the Catholics in the province of Nova Scotia have anything to complain of in respect of the treatment which they receive from their Protestant brethren. I believe they are fairly, and justly and honourably treated, and I think I can appeal to my Roman Catholic friends from the province of Nova Scotia to bear witness to the accuracy of what I now state.
What are the arguments of the right hon. leader of the opposition in 1896? That this matter had better be left to the people of Manitoba; and, following the advent of his party to power, certain negotiations were carried on between his government and the government of Manitoba. I am not disposed to-(Jay to enter into a consideration of how far the agreement arrived at, was or was not satisfactory; but I do say that the Homan Catholics of the province of Manitoba constitute a larger proportion of the people of that province, than the Roman Catholics of this Dominion constitute of the population of the Dominion as a whole; and we cannot for a moment, suppose that- the influence of the Roman Catholics in the province of Manitoba in the advocacy of what they consider to be their just rights and for the redress of any grievances from which they suffer will be any less powerful than it would be in relation to the enactment of ordinances under the provisions of the Northwest Territories Act, chapter 62, of the Revised Statutes of Canada. I trust that I make myself perfectly clear. The Roman Catholics of the province of Manitoba are in a minority in that province; but they are a more powerful minority in the province of Manitoba than the Roman Catholics, as a whole, are in this whole Dominion, and I have absolutely no doubt that the majority of the people of Manitoba will he disposed to. deal fairly, honourably and generously with them, just as the people of the province of Nova Scotia, without anv statutory provision whatever, have dealt fairly, honourably and generously with the Roman Catholics of that province.
Then a suggestion has been made that it would be desirable for the parliament of Canada, in enacting this measure, to attempt to place restrictions upon the legislative authority of the legislature of Manitoba in respect of the territory proposed to be added. In the territory there are at the present time, not more than 165 white people, 400 or 500 half-breeds, and the balance of the population are Indians. Now, a proposal to place any such restriction upon Manitoba would seem to me to be an impossible one, for two reasons. In the first place, I

do not believe that it is politically possible, because I do not believe that Manitoba would accept the extension of her boundaries coupled with any such restriction. In the next place, I do not think it is constitutionally possible. I would like to point out to hon. members, to whose attention this may not have been brought, that the provisions of the British North America Act, of 1871, .with regard to the constitution of a province in the first instance, are very different from those contained in the clause of the same Act, providing for the altera- * tion of the boundaries of a province. Section 2 of that Act is as follows:
The parliament of Canada may from time to time establish new provinces in any territories forming for the time being part of the Dominion of Canada but not included in any. province thereof, and may, at the time of such establishment, make provision for the constitution and administration of any such province, and for the passing of laws for the peace, order and good government of such province and for its representation in the said parliament.
But when we come to the third section of that statute, we find that the language with regard to increasing the area of a province, is in very different terms. It is as follows :
The parliament of Canada may from time to time, with the consent of the legislature of any province of the said Dominion, increase, diminish, or otherwise alter ' the limits of such province, upon such terms and conditions as may be agreed to bv the said legislature, and may, with the like consent, make provision respecting the effect and operation of any such increase or diminution or alteration of territory in relation to any province affected thereby.
We have in the one section direct authority for this parliament to determine the constitution of a province. In the other section we have not any such thing, and it seems to me absolutely impossible to conceive that you can have a province in Canada, such as Manitoba would be after this Bill had passed, which would be governed as to one part of it by one constitutional provision in respect of education, and in another part of it, by another constitutional provision in respect of education. I do not believe that the British North America Act of 1871 contemplated any such thing. To my mind, it is inconceivable, and I do not find warrant for it m the statute. It is inconceivable that you could have one constitutional limitation in old Manitoba and another constitutional limitation in the part of Manitoba which we now propose to add. But whether I am right or wrong in believing that that is constitutionally impracticable, I am absolutely certain that it is politically impracticable : and I venture to say that the people of Manitoba, imbued as they are
with big, broad, generous spirit, would be inclined to deal with their fellow countrymen who may be of a different faith in the same broad-minded and generous spirit as that which has been evinced in other provinces of Canada where no constitutional provisions of this kind exist. So, Mr. Speaker, I venture to say that this Bill which we have submitted to the parliament of Canada is along the right lines-along the lines of observing the constitution of Canada as it is embodied in the British North America Act, of 1867, and in the British North America Act of 1871. My hon. friend the Postmaster General last evening cited competent authorities for the position that in so far as any rights do exist in the territory which we propose to add to the province of Manitoba, those will remain to be dealt with by the parliament of Canada in so far as such matters appertain to the parliament of Canada or by the legislature of the province of Manitoba in so far as they appertain to the legislature of the province of Manitoba. 1 venture to think that the course which the government has taken in that regard is one in the best interests of all concerned, and will commend itself, not only to the majority of this parliament, but to the majority of the people of Canada as well.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That subsection 1 of section 4 be struck out, and the following substituted therefor -.
4.	Inasmuch as the province was not in debt at the time that the province was established, it shall be entitled to be paid and to receive from the government of Canada Iby half-yearly payments, in advance, on the \first days of January and July in each year, an annual sum not exceeding $381,584.19, being the equivalent of interest at the rate of five per cent per annum on the sum of $7,631,6S3,-85, the difference between a principal sum of $8,107,500 and $475,816.15 heretofore advanced by the government to the province for provincial purposes; and such amount shall be fixed and determined by the Governor in Council after the holding of a conference by (the federal government with the premiers of the different provinces of Canada in respect thereto, and also in respect to any increases in the debt allowance which it would he just and equitable to make to the other provinces of Canada in connection with the increase of the debt allowance to the said province of Manitoba.
My hon. friend will see that the amounts are exactly the same as in the section as proposed. The only difference is that the Governor in Council may pay an amount not exceeding this, the amount to he settled after there has been a conference between the federal government and the premiers of the different provinces of Canada called to consider this matter and also to consider what allowance, if any, it would be just and equitable to make to the other provinces of Canada in connection with the increase in the debt allowance to the province of Manitoba.
I think that the idea of a provincial conference to consider and if possible to settle and determine what shall be the subsidies granted to the different provinces of Canada is one which ought to commend itself to every member of this House. We know that a good many years ago there

was a conference of the provincial governments held at the city of Quebec in, I think, the year 1886. That conference was not called by the federal government, it was convened at the instance of the two larger provinces and certain resolutions were passed looking to a readjustment of the subsidies from the Dominion to the provinces. Their resolutions were sent to Ottawa, but they were not acted upon and so far as the public records show they were not even considered. In 1906 there was a new departure and the government determined to call the premiers of the different provinces of Canada in conference with a view to considering the various claims that were being made by the provinces upon the Dominion and more especially to consider the question of increasing the subsidy allowances to the different provinces. I think that was a move in the interests of the whole Dominion. The different provinces are like a family, they together constitute this nation and I cannot imagine anything more calculated to promote harmony and good will between the different provinces of Canada and to allay dissatisfaction than for the federal government to summon the different provincial governments in conference with a view to talking over matters which are of common interest and to settle any questions that may exist in relation to the financial status of the different provinces. That was the first time in the history of confederation that such a conference was called by the federal government. The act of summoning the conference was received with universal approval by the people of Canada. All the governments of Canada responded to the invitation and the provinces were all represented at that conference. They entered upon their deliberations with a sincere desire to come to conclusions which would be just and equitable to all the provinces and which would be in the general interest of Canada.
I think myself that the government could not take a step more in the interest of the whole people of Canada than to follow the example which was set in 1906, and now summon a conference of the Premiers of the different provinces. To-day we have this spectacle of one province coming to the federal government and claiming that the arrangements which were made twenty-five years ago with that province are at the present time unsatisfactory, and claiming what in effect is an additional subsidy; because, no matter how we may speak of it, there is no doubt that the addition to the debt allowance is an addition to the subsidy of the province. It is in no way connected with the question of ownership of the public domain, it is a question which pertains as much to all the other provinces of Canada as it does to Manitoba. We have also the spectacle to-day of the province of British Columbia coming to this government and appealing for better terms, and we have a proposal on the part of this government, in effect, to leave the claims of that province to arbitration under an arrangement by which this government would appoint one commissioner, the province of British Columbia another commissioner, and these two commissioners appoint a third. Now, it does seem to me that instead of dealing with each province by itself, there ought to be a conference of the Premiers of all the provinces meeting here in Ottawa, who would confer from day to day with the federal government, and who, I am sure, would enter upon that conference with a disposition to deal justly and fairly the one with the other, and to reach conclusiohs which would be in their nature final, and would give general satisfaction to all the provinces of Canada.
Has my non. friend overlooked a statement made by the Prime, Minister on the second reading of the Bill, dealing exactly with the question to which he is now' referring?
What is that?

I will read it if the hon. gentleman will permit me. The Prime Minister said on March 4, page 4350:
And I would like to repeat what I have already said in speaking upon the resolutions in that regard, that when we do come to consider that proposal I think it will be just and necessary to give some consideration to the maritime provinces whose boundaries cannot be enlarged by reason of their natural situation, to call them into our councils and give to them a just voice as to the terms upon which these lands should be handed over, and especially with regard to what compensation, if any, should be given to the three maritime provinces by reason of the transfer of these lands to the governments of Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan.

1 had that well in mind, I had not overlooked it at all. But my hon. friend will see that these remarks of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister apply simply to the question of giving compensation to the maritime provinces by reason of handing over at some time in the future, whether the near future or the distant future, the public domain of the three prairie provinces. Now, that may be a long time hence, that cannot be done without some arrangement with these three provinces by themselves. As the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Rogers), admitted when he was addressing the House, when it comes to dealing with that question, it would be for the governments of those provinces to say what amount of money

they would return to the federal treasury in exchange for the lands to be handed over to them. That is a matter that can only be dealt w'ith by arrangement with the three provinces. It was stated by the Minister of the Interior that there are a good many people in the prairie provinces who would prefer to have the money instead of the lands, the money which they can use for ordinary purposes of public improvement, and they would prefer to let the Dominion government administer the prairie lands and give them away to the settler free of any charge, as they have been doing in the past. Many people in the prairie provinces believe that instead of making the prairie lands a source of revenue, they should be given aw7ay absolutely free to the man who is prepared to come into that country, and make a home for himself and his family. Therefore, it may be many, many years before that question would come up if it is only to come up as suggested by the Prime Minister.
Is the hon. geni cm an disposed to leave to the dim and distant future the settlement of all these questions with the provinces by the sea?

No, I am not disposed to leave it to the dim and distant future. I say that now, when we are altering the situation of three important provinces of Canada, when we are trebling the area of the province of Manitoba, when we are almost doubling the area, if not quite doubling the area, of the province of Ontario, and when we are almost quadrupling the area of the province of Quebec, when we are altering the financial terms under which the province of Manitoba for 26 years has been in the confederation, I say that now is the time to take up the question as to what, if any, consideration should be given to the maritime provinces.
Now, if ever, is the time to take up the question of what should be done in regard to. the representation of the maritime provinces. It does seem to me that those of us who are here representing the maritime provinces can appeal with great force to the representatives of those great, strong and growing provinces of Canada, to give fair and reasonable consideration to the claims of the maritime provinces, not only the financial claims but their claims in respect to representation. My hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) suggests that we should leave it until the time comes to deal w'ith the public domain of the three prairie provinces. Why, Sir, within a year or two at the outside, there ought to be introduced into this parliament a redistribution Bill. Under that Bill, unless some provision is made with regard to the representation of the maritime provinces, these three small provinces by the sea will Mr. PUGSLEY.
lose five representatives; the province of Nova Scotia will lose two, New Brunswick wil] lose two, and Prince Edw'ard Island will lose one. That small province of Prince Edward Island, small though it may be, is yet a province composed of men the equal of any of the people of Canada, that province which, when solicited to join the union, declined to enter unless it was assured of a representation of six members, a representation which the people of Prince Edward Island were led to believe would never be reduced; that province today will find, as a result of the redistribution which must before long be passed through this parliament, her representation in the House of Commons reduced by cne-half the representation which it was stipulated she should be allowed by the Act when she entered confederation. Now In New Brunswick we shall find as a result of the redistribution that our representation will be reduced to eleven, and that of Nova Scotia will be reduced to sixteen. I say, therefore, that now is the time, when we are dealing with these important constitutional questions, to take up this matter and endeavour to settle it. We know that the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia have asked for a conference of the Premiers of the different nrovinces for the purpose of considering this question of representation.
They all feel in the strongest possible manner that that question ought to be dealt w'ith at a conference of the provinces. Would it not be entirely opportune, that, in connection with the financial question and in connection with the extension of the boundaries this question of representation should be taken up? It will not delay this measure very long. It would only mean that it would stand over until the next session of Parliament. A conference could be called very soon after Parliament rises, representatives of the provinces could easily be got together and all these important matters could be gone into by the premiers of the different provinces in consultation with the federal government. I have sufficient confidence in the good judgment and in the spirit of generosity of the various provincial governments to believe that they will consent to an arrangement which will give-and this is all we ask- to the lower provinces that representation that we had when we entered into the union, all we ask is that our representation should not be reduced below what it was when these provinces entered the confederacy.^ We do not ask for any increase. We are willing to let our rights to an increase depend on an increase in population. In saying that I speak, not for Liberals, not for Conservatives, but for the whole people of New Brunswick and I believe I speak the united voice of the whole people of

the maritime provinces, when 1 plead-
I suppose I cannot demand, because the older provinces have the right, perhaps on their side, to stand by the strict terms of the Act of Union-for fair play in the proper sense of the word.
I plead" for doing away with the injustice from which we are suffering and for removing many of the disadvantages which are pressing upon our people. I desire to express my most sincere thanks to my hon. friend who sits on my right (Mr. Lemieux) who, this afternoon, in a true spirit of generosity, in a spirit which makes for the advantage of the whole people of Canada, said that he would welcome the day when justice would be done to the maritime provinces with respect to its representation and when an Act would be passed which would prevent. its suffering any loss in representation. Let me appeal to my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen). I have heard him before on this question and I have heard him speak in eloquent terms of the injustice from which the maritime provinces have been suffering and the great necessity of doing something to take away this injustice and the certainty of continued loss in representation. Let me ask him whether he has taken the question up with his colleagues and, if he has,_ if he entertains the same view to-day which he entertained when he was a member of the provincial legislature. Let me ask him if he can conceive of any better time than now to take up this question of the representation of the maritime provinces, if he can conceive any better time for its consideration by a conference of the provinces *when they might be summoned, as they could be summoned now, if this measure stands over, to consider all these questions, to consider how the enlargement of the territories of three great provinces of Canada affects the smaller provinces, to consider how the alteration in the financial terms affects the smaller provinces, and to consider whether or not in its material aspects the alteration of the constitutions of these three provinces affects the question of representation and ought now to be dealt with. In my humble judgment there never was a time in the past so appropriate as now to take up this question of representation and there never will be a time so opportune in the future as is the present occasion for taking up the subject and dealing with it.
My hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Rogers) sought to justify this special dealing with the province of Manitoba by the statement that all the members of the Interprovincial Conference approved of these claims on the part of Manitoba, and he said that Manitoba had no greater friend at that conference than myself. Well, Mr. Chairman, I have always,
I am proud to be able to say, been a friend * of Manitoba. I was one of the pioneers of Manitoba. My hon. friend speaks of the pioneers, and my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. White) speaks of the pathfinders. When I went to Manitoba there were many pathfinders, but of later years, and I believe since the time when the hon' Minister of the Interior went into Manitoba, the hardships have all passed away and there is no pleasanter place in which to live than Manitoba. The people suffer no more hardships there than they do in the other provinces of Canada. Manitoba is an exceedingly prosperous province. But while I was then a friend of Manitoba and desirous of doing justice to that province as one member of the Interprovincial Conference, yet I beg to differ from my hon. friend and to say to the committee that the records show, if I read the records aright, that my hon. friend is entirely mistaken when he says that the members of the Interprovincial Conference approved of these claims of Manitoba. I can prove what I say by the record. If the members of the committee will take up the sessional papers of 1907 they will find a full report of the proceedings of the Interprovincial Conference. I refer them specially to sessional paper 29a.
Report of proceedings in conference between members of the government of Canada and of the various provincial governments assembled at Ottawa, October, 1906:
At that conference the first and principle question which was dealt with was an increase in the subsidies to the various provinces, and if hon. gentlemen will look at the return they will find, upon the fourth page ' Resolutions of the Conference,' dealing with this subject of an increase in subsidies. My hon. friend the Minister of the Interior has endeavoured to make the committee believe that, while these resolutions were agreed to, yet, at the same time, the members of the conference approved of the special claims which the province of Manitoba was making. I say they did not, and I speak as a member of the conference, not only from my recollection but from the record as contained in that return which was brought down to parliament. This is what the conference resolved:
Therefore it is unanimously resolved that the subject matter of the resolutions adopted by the conference of the representatives of the several provinces held at Quebec-, in December 1902 and which was shortly thereafter presented to the government of the Dominion and which were ratified by the legislature of the then existing provinces except that of British Columbia, he now pressed upon the government of the Dominion for immediate and favourable action, under reserve of the right of any province to now submit to such government, memoranda in writing concerning any claims it may have to larger sums

than those set out in the said resolutions, or to additional consideration or recognition.
My hon. friend did not give that weight to the word ' now ' which the conference intended should be given to it and which must necessarily be given to it. What the members of the conference did was, first, to pass a resolution in regard to a general increase of subsidies amongst the different provinces. Then they said: We are prepared to consider the special case of any province and we reserve to the government of any province the right to now submit a memorandum of any special claims which they may have. The province of British Columbia did submit its claim for additional consideration. That memorandum applied as well to the province of British Columbia as to the province of Manitoba and to every other province in the Dominion. British Columbia, as I have said, submitted its claim and what did we do with it ? The conference unanimously rejected it, and the two representatives from the province of Manitoba, Mr. Roblin and Mr. Campbell, joined in an unanimous recommendation that the claims of British Columbia should not be conceded. That is the way in which the conference dealt with that special claim-a claim in respect to which these reasons apply just as much as they do to the claim of the province of Manitoba. The conference rejected, as I have said, the claim of British Columbia, but, in view of the exceptional conditions in that province, in view of its being a mountainous country and road-making being exceedingly expensive, and in view of other considerations which were put forward in the memorandum and which will be found in this return, the conference recommended that the Dominion should give to the province of British Columbia an additional allowance of $100,000 per year for a period of ten years.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not quite understand how these matters are settled by the conference; do they vote by provinces or by individual membership?
They voted by individual membership, but I may say that they were unanimous.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Was the membership for each province restricted.

No, the representatives for Ontario were Sir J. P. Whitney, Mr. Foy, and Mr. Matheson; for Quebec, Sir Lomer Gouin, Mr. Turgeon and Mr. Weir; for Nova Scotia, Mr. Murray and Mr. Drys-dale; for New Brunswick, Mr. Tweedie and Mr. Pugsley; for Prince Edward Island, Mr. Peters and Mr. George E. Hughes; for Manitoba, Mr. Roblin and Mr. Campbell; for British Columbia, Mr. McBride; for Saskatchewan, Mr. Walter Scott and Mr. Calder; for Alberta, Mr. Rutherford and

r Mr. Cross. For each of the larger provinces there were three representatives and t from the other provinces two representat-, ives each, except British Columbia which , had one representative in the person of , the Prime Minister. So far as I remember the resolutions at the conference were | passed unanimously. In order to show t that the conference had no thought of J. approving of any additional claims of the , province of Manitoba I find , in the return . a memorandum which was submitted by [ Sir J. P. Whitney, the Hon. J. J. Foy, anil L the Hon. A. J. Matheson, in which there is this language:
. We urge that in the future no special grant t at any rate should be made to any one province. We repeat that in our opinion an ' agreement which will render impossible ' periodical applications for the rearrangement ' of the subsidy is feasible and should be de-* termined upon. It is possible that such an arrangement might be fixed and positive and at the same time elastic, working automatically so as to speak as the Dominion census from, time to time would determine.
There you have a strong protest on the part of the representatives from Ontario, which protest was concurred in by the members of the conference against in the future making, any special grant to any one province. And, so I say, at that conference it was intended to deal with the various claims that were submitted and to make a finality of them so far as the conference could do. The conference was of the opinion expressed by Messrs. Whitney, Foy and Matheson that in future there 'should be no special grant to any one province.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Did the conference come to any resolution on that question?

No, not so far as the returns show. The only exception from that was with respect to British Columbia where they thought that owing to special circumstances they should recommend an additional allowance of $100,000 a year for ten years. My recollection is that the representatives of Manitoba with the representatives of the other provinces, felt that the Dominion was dealing generously at that time with the different provinces, but at all events the special claim of Manitoba was not further mentioned at the conference, and we were not called upon to deal with it. The conference having agreed upon the general resolution as to the increase in subsidy then reserved the right to any province to, at that time, not in the future, submit its claims to the government so that the conference might deal with them. In response to that invitation the province of British Columbia did submit its claim which was dealt with by the conference in the manner I have described, but the province of Manitoba did not re-

spond to the invitation and did not present any other claim, and I was under the impression that the representatives of Manitoba went home perfectly satisfied that they had received the same generous treatment which the other provinces had received in connection with the adjustment of the subsidies. I do not know that it would be of any advantage to take up the time of the committee in urging that there is no fair ground whatever for now dealing specially with the one province of Manitoba any more than there is for dealing with any other province of the Dominion which might be picked out. Reference has already been made to the fact that it is now proposed to arbitrarily give to the province of Manitoba a sum of about $32 a head upon a population of about 250,000. Why not make it the actual population of 450,000? In the case of British Columbia it was fixed oni a population of 60,000, and although British Columbia to-day has a population of about 350,000, I am not aware that it has received any increase other than the general increase which was made in 1884. The government fixed upon a population of 250,000 for Manitoba, because they say that parliament in 1905 made a debt allowance based upon a population of 250,000 for the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. But, you ignore British Columbia, you ignore Ontario, you ignore Quebec, you ignore Nova Scotia, and simply because in 1905 when two new provinces were being created, these provinces were given an estimated population of about 250,000, you say it is right to do the same thing now in respect to an old province which has been forty years a member of the confederacy. The government ignores absolutely the fact that this eight million dollars which it is proposed to give to the province of Manitoba does not represent one single dollar of expenditure made before Manitoba became a member of the confederacy.
They admit that Manitoba had no debt when she became a part of the union. They ignore the fact that every dollar of the debt allowances of Ontario and Quebec, if I remember rightly, represented money of the people of the old province of Canada which had been paid out for the construction of public works which were handed over to the Dominion, and which form to-day a most valuable asset of the Dominion, such as the great system of canals which are essential factors in the system of national transportation, and in respect of which those provinces did not receive one dollar of interest, because that allowance simply goes to pay the interest on the debt which they incurred before confederation, in order to, construct public works which are for the general advantage of Canada. They ignore altogether the
fact that the larger part of the debt allowances for the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick was incurred in respect of works of a national character which passed over to the Dominion, works which, if those provinces had not constructed them before confederation, such as custom houses, post offices, railways, harbour works and lighthouses, would have had to be constructed and paid for by the whole people of Canada. Hon. gentlemen ignore these facts altogether, and treat the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia1 in this light and cavalier manner, just as if they had no claim for consideration in a readjustment of the debt allowance of a province. The hon. gentleman said that there was a precedent for this. What was the precedent he cited? He cited the case of the province of Nova Scotia in 1869, when an increase was made to the debt allowance of that province. The members of the government of that day most of whom had taken part in drawing up the compact of confederation, said: We recognize that this is something which ought not to be done except in a case of the gravest possible necessity. But they admitted that a mistake had been made in respect of Nova Scotia. Nova Scotia's debt allowance was based on what was assumed to be her actual expenditure on public works up to the time of the Quebec conference; but between that time and the time of her coming into the union, she had expended $2,000,000 or $3,000,000 in extending her railway system; and it was agreed that because ot that mistake, parliament ought to interfere and put her in the position in which she would have been placed if that mistake had not taken place. Sir Charles Tupper, then Dr. Tupper, made a strong argument in favour of rectifying the mistake, and showed how it had occurred. This has been done also in the case of Manitoba, under circumstances which were explained during the debate on the motion for the second reading of the Bill.

Yes.
