Those terms were simply based upon the necessities which would arise by reason of the addition of territory.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Why were not the other provinces entitled to be heard?

I am prepared to admit that they ought to have been heard, but we cannot always have our own way. My

right hon. friend who leads the opposition will remember that I urged almost from the day I came into the government that some steps should be taken to secure the representation of the maritime provinces at the numbers at which it stood at the time of confederation. I did not succeed at that time, but I had a great hope of succeeding -when the time came for dealing fully with this question of boundaries. The time had not arrived when the late government was in power, although my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition went a considerable distance in that direction when a resolution was passed to enlarge the boundaries of the province of Quebec, and a clause with his approval was added providing that the increased territory should in no way affect the representation of the other provinces; in other wolds, that, in estimating the 65 members who form the pivot upon which the representation turns, the added territory should not be _ taken into account at all. That was quite a step forward, and I had certainly strong hope that when we came to deal effectually with the matter, the claims of the maritime provinces with regard to representation -would be recognized. A short time ago, I think in the discussion on the address in reply to the speech from the Throne, my hon. friend from Queens, P.E.I. (Mr. McLean), took strong ground that something ought to be done. Is his voice to be heard now, or is he going to allow this Bill to pass without raising a protest on behalf of the province from which he comes, and which is suffering so much by reason of loss of representation? We heard at the same time from my hon. friend from Kings and Albert (Mr. Fowler), who, I regret, from circumstances over which he has no control, is not able to be here to-night; and I had hoped that he also would raise his voice against the continuance of the present condition of affairs with respect to the representation of the maritime provinces. There is nothing more that I can say; the facts are plain" With respect to the province of New Brunswick, the Dominion of Canada has an asset which cost that province upwards of $5,000,000, and which to-day is yielding a revenue to this country. That is charged as a part of the debt account, and New Brunswick is not receiving one cent of interest in respect of that indebtedness. All that the Dominion has done has been to pay the interest on the indebtedness incurred in the construction of that revenue-producing property. In respect to Manitoba, hon. gentlemen propose today to fix arbitrarily $8,000,000 as her allowance, and to grant her on this account $400,000 yearly out of the Dominion treasury. I may be undulv prejudiced as repre-Mr. PUGSLEY.	j
senting one of the smaller provinces down by the sea, but it does seem to me that there are claims in respect of those provinces- financial claims and claims in respect to altering the basis of representation- -which ought to be considered. If my right hon. friend passes all the legislation now proposed, and leaves unsettled these questions, which are believed by the people of the maritime provinces to be vital to their future, he is going to have great difficulty in dealing with them in the future.
As I have said now is the time, when we are dealing with these important constitutional qeustions, to call together the government of the different provinces of Canada to a conference, confer with them, let . them meet with each other- the representatives of all parts of Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific-let them confer together, in conjunction with the members of the federal government, and I am sure they will bring to bear their best intelligence, bring to" bear their mutual desire to make an arrangement which will promote peace and harmony among all the people of Canada. If that is done I have every confidence that they will work out a plan which will be satisfactory to all the provinces, and which will be satisfactory to this parliament and to the government of Canada.
Mr. HUGHES (Kings County, P.E.I.) I have very great pleasure indeed in seconding the motion which has been made by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugs-ley), and I agree with every statement he has presented to the committee. I think that I can make -some other statements that will appeal to the fairness of this committee, particularly with regard to the province of Prince Edward Island. I am bound to say that there are many features of this Bill which appeal to me" as being fair and reasonable. The statements made on behalf of the government that, in the preparation of this Bill and in the giving of financial terms to the province of Manitoba they desired to put that province on a. footing of equality, so far as regards financial terms with the sister provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, appeal to me. That desire appears to me, so far as I understand it, to be fair and reasonable provided you do no injustice to any of the other provinces in the making of that arrangement. Sir, I look upon the confederation as a partnership, a partnership of nine members. Every one of these members has a private business of his own which he is carrying on, and if you take from the partnership funds a large sum of money and give it to any one of the partners for the purpose of his Own private business you necessarily, to that extent, do

some injustice to all the other partners unless they receive compensation in some other way. Sir, unless this confederation, this partnership, is carried on by the application of principle of the strictest justice it would appear to me that it cannot be carried on at all satisfactorily, that you are introducing a system that sooner or later will have very dangerous results. Now, while the granting to Manitoba of additional territory so that its area will be practically the same as that of the sister provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta appeals to me, and while I think that by placing all these prairie provinces on a similar financial basis you are not going far astray, at the same time to date these payments to Manitoba back to 1908 appears to me to be quite unjustifiable. That is the feature of this Bill that I cannot understand and cannot see the justice of. I want to consider the case of Prince Edward Island and to refer to the special conditions connected with that province. Prince Edward Island never had any Crown lands or mines or minerals, and in that respect she stands exactly on the same footing as the three prairie provinces. Therefore, I think that when large additions have been made to the finanical resources of Manitoba, that the position of Prince Edward Island ought to be specially considered. We will take up one! item in this Bill, which I think will prove that a very great injustice will be done to the province of Prince Edward Island unless this special provision is taken into consideration. I refer now to the sum that is to be paid to the province of Manitoba in lieu of the public lands. The sum of $562,500, based upon the population, is to be given to Manitoba	in lieu of public lands, and
that sum is to be increased from time to time. That payment amounts to practically-as near as I can figure it out -$1.25 per head of the population of Manitoba at the present time. When Prince Edward Island came into confederation her allowance because of the fact that she had no public lands was $45,000, which amounts to less than 50 cents per head of her population. If we want to be fair to the province of Prince Edward Island we must I think-and in this matter I appeal to every member of this committee-increase the allowance to that province to make it correspond with the payment which we are now giving to Manitoba. Prince Edward Island, therefore ought to receive $1.25 per head of her population by reason of having no public lands, mines or minerals. That would be an addition of $75,000 to her present subsidy. Furthermore, if you pay these subsidies to the province of Manitoba from the year 1908, by every reason of justice and fair play yuu ought to likewise pay this additional subsidy to the
province of Prince Edward Island from that year.
Hear, hear.

This would give her arrears of $300,000. It seems to me that that is a fair and businesslike statement which ought to appeal to the fairness and justice of the Minister of Finance. I might also state, as it has been referred to by the member for St. John, that when the older provinces came into confederation they brought in with them their public works for which they had paid. The same thing applies to the province of Prince Edward Island. We built our own railway in Prince Edward Island before we came into confederation and paid for it, and the cost of that railway was charged to us in the allowance that was given to us at the time of confederation. At the time of our entry into confederation the debt of Canada was $49.40 per head of the population, and Prince Edward Island was given a debt allowance of $50 per head of the population. That was charged to her, and the province was also charged with every dollar expended on public works and we have since that time paid the interest on our debt, which includes the cost of building the railway, and our share of the debt of the Dominion of Canada. That is a fair arrangement, and I have no fault to find with it, but it has been sometimes said to me, and the view is held even by some members of this House, that the Dominion of Canada built the railway on Prince Edward Island and presented it to the province as a gift. Nothing of the kind. We came in under exactly the same conditions as the other provinces of Canada.
A word with regard to representation. That is a question of very great importance to the smaller provinces of this Dominion. Some few years ago, when I had the honour of a seat in this House, I brought that question each year to the attention of the House and was glad to find that each time it was received with better attention and received greater support and when in 1907 I moved a resolution asking that an address be presented to His Majesty praying that he would submit a measure to the imperial parliament changing the British North America Act to the exent that none of the three Atlantic provinces in the Dominion of Canada should have fewer representatives than it had at the time it entered confederation, my resolution receive very generous support from hon. gentlemen opposite, including the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Borden), the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain), the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Lalor), the hon. member for the Niagara District

'(Mr. Lancaster), and I think the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. Stanfield).

They have a provision of that kind in the constitution of Australia, and British Columbia secured such a condition under the terms of her entrance, into the confederation. The time has surely come when the government of this country should seriously consider this problem in relation to the maritime provinces. I want the Minister of Finance to consider what I have said with reference to the financial terms in regard to the position of Prince Edward Island. It appears to me that the case need only be stated for its justice to _ be apparent, and that the claim of Prince Edward Island for treatment similar to that now being given to Manitoba is insuperable. I feel sure that the members of the government will not see injustice done to any province, particularly to any of the smaller provinces, and it must be remembered that Prince Edward Island stands in exactly the same position, as far as public lands go, as Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. I submit this matter with all confidence to the consideration of the government and hope that they will deal with it. speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) made some remarks with reference to the representation of the maritime provinces in the parliament of Canada, having -regard to the fact that after each decennial census for some decades there has ibeen a decrease in the representation of those provinces. The hon. gentleman made a direct reference to myself and stated that he had heard me in the past speaking in very strong language as to the injustice that was being done to the lower provinces in consequence of their 'osing representation because of the fact *hat the population in the lower provinces was not increasing as rapidly as that of the other provinces in confederation.
Therefore, under the terms under which we entered the confederation in 1867, we were jlosing representation, as we were not holding our own proportionately with the population of the province of Quebec. My hon. friend asked me if I still entertained the same views on that question which I entertained at the time to which he referred, which was a time when my hon. friend and myself both occupied seats in the local legislature of the province of New Brunswick, and in which, on several Mr. HUGHES (Kings, P.E.I.).
occasions, this question of the loss of representation was discussed. I would say to my hon. friend that I still hold precisely the same-views that I held when I was a member of the legislature of the province of New Brunswick. I think it is a most desirable thing, and an act of simple justice, that some effective action should be taken under which there should be provided at least an irreducible minimum so far as the representation of the maritime provinces of Canada is concerned. My hon. friend brought the matter to the attention of the New Brunswick legislature on several occasions when he was a member of a government of that province. On one occasion he made the contention that if a case was properly submitted to the highest court in the empire he believed that court would hold that the proper interpretation of the word ' Canada ' in the British North America Act, in the clauses concerning representation of the various provinces, was that Canada consisted of the four original provinces of the confederacy, and that as a result of such an interpretation we would not lose any part of our representation, and that what we had lost would tie restored to us. My hon. friend then Attorney General of the province of New Brunswick, carried the matter first to the Supreme Court of Canada, and afterwards <o the Privy Council; but the Privy Council failed to uphold the contention of my hon. Mend, I regret to say. His contention was that the word ' Canada ' mentioned in the British North America Act, was the Canada consisting of the four original provinces of the confederacy; that contention was dismissed by the Privy Council, and it was held that the loss of representation which we had sustained was justified under the British North America Act, Now, my hon. friend has referred to the fact that it is a matter of great regret to us in the lower provinces that this is the case. It is indeed a matter of great regret; to ,us, irrespective of party. The provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick were two of the original provinces of the confederacy, whose consent made it possible to bring about the union, and which at that time did not anticipate the tremendous growth and expansion of the west, and it is, I say, a matter of regret to us that our representation after every census has been reduced, and we fear that perhaps that reduction will continue to go on in the future. Now, this question is not a new one in the parliament of Canada. We find that on January 31, 1910, a resolution was moved in this House by the hon. gentleman who then and now, represents the county of Bichmond in the province of Nova Scotia (Mr. Kyte). That resolution was in this language:

That in the opinion of this House the maritime provinces of Canada should have preserved to them the representation in the House of Commons that they now enjoy. That in the redistribution of the constituencies to be made after the next decennial 'census the number of representatives to be [DOT]returned from the said provinces should not ,in any case be reduced. And that an humble petition be presented to His Majesty praying ,that the British North America Act be amended in accordance writh the purport of this resolution.
That resolution was debated, and an amendment was moved by an hon. gentleman who at that time, represented the county of Queens, Prince Edward Island, (Mr. Warburton), and it was seconded by Dr. Daniel, then representing the city of St. John. That amendment read as follows:
Each province in the Dominion of Canada .should have as a minimum representation in the House of Commons the representation it had upon becoming a province of Canada. That in the redistribution of the constituencies to be made after the next and after every future decennial census, the representation of each province should be not less than that minimum. And that a humble petition be presented to His Majesty praying that the British North America Act be amended in accordance with the purport of this resolution.
The resolution moved by the member for Richmond was to the effect that the representation of the provinces should not fall below the representation which they had at the time this resolution was moved. The amendment of the hon. member for Queens, Prince 'Edward Island, was to the effect that the representation of none of the provinces of Canada should at any time, fall below what that representation was at the time they entered the union. That amendment was debated in this House, a number of hon. gentlemen took part in the debate, and among others, was. my hon. friend from the city of St. John (Mr. Pugsley). I am a little surprised to find, on referring to his speech, that it lacked in large measure, the enthusiasm that we used to hear him express on this subject, when he spoke upon it in the legis-ature of the province of New Brunswick. Those who heard the extremely strong views which the hon gentleman entertained before he went to the Privy Council, and the even stronger views to which he gave expression after he returned from the Privy Council, when in that legislature, he criticised the judgment, and pointed out wherein he thought it was weak, and maintained that the province had a grievance which called for redress, believed that when She hon. gentleman came here, and became a member of the government of Canada in the year 1907, only a short time would elapse before he would so influence his colleagues in the House and in the government, that some remedial legislation would be introduced to redress the grievances under which he and many of us felt, that we were labouring under in the lower provinces. But we find that the hon. gentleman, so far as the record goes, did not lift his voice or use his great influence in that direction. We find that when the bon. gentleman addressed the House on the resolution moved by the hon. member for Richmond, and the amendment moved by the member for Queens, Prince Edward Island, that enthusiasm which had so marked the hon. gentleman's speeches in the House of Assembly of New Brunswick bad practically disappeared, that a change had come over the spirit of the hon. gentleman's dreams, and he no longer talked of the injustice that was being done to the lower provinces. Let me quote some of the remarks of the hon. gentleman on that occasion:
, In my opinion the way in which this matter should be presented is rather along the line taken by my hon friend (Mr. Richards) than along that taken by my hon friend from York (Mr. Crocket). My hon. friend from York said that a great injustice was done tfie maritime provinces, and he claims that these provinces were not here asking for a favour but demanding as a matter of right that a change should be made in the representation.
If my hon friend will pardon me, I said we were demanding the restoration of a right of which we had been deprived.

I understood the hon gentleman to say, and I think I understood him correctly, that it is not as a matter of favour, but rather as a matter of right that the representation should be restored to what it was. But it seems to me that my hon. friend from Prince (Mr. Richards) has put the matter on the only ground on which it can be put, and that is that it would be a generous thing for the larger provinces to recognize the dissatisfaction existing in the maritime provinces and which is bound to increase as our representation declines. It would be an act of broad generosity for the larger provinces to recognize that fact, to deal in this spirit with the smaller provinces, and to restore the representation to what it was at the time of confederation and below which the people then thought it never would fall.
The reason that I say it cannot be 6a.id that an injustice has been done to the lower provinces is that we have no right to complain of what is the interpretation given to the constitution by the highest court of the realm.
It will, therefore, be seen that the. bon. gentleman, speaking of the resolution in this House, took a distinctly different ground from the ground which he took in speaking on a similar subject in the legislature of New Brunswick at a time when he was a member of the government of that province. This resolution, as I

say, was discussed by a number of members from the different provinces, and all the speeches were distinctly sympathetic. The right hon. the leader of the opposition, then first minister, addressed the House. I have not had time to go through the reports as I did not know the question was coming up to-night, but I did read the report of the debate some years ago, and 1 believe that every man expressed sympathy with the position that was taken by the lower provinces. The right hon. the leader of the opposition said that the question was one which could not be disposed of by this parliament, that the question of representation had been settled by the British North America Act, that it was a compact entered into by the different provinces, that the question was one which would have to be dealt with by the different provinces, and a conclusion come to by them in regard to the matter, before it could be taken up and dealt with by the government of the Dominion, and before a change could be asked for in the British North America Act. Following that session I had a conference with a gentleman who was at that time the premier of Prince Edward Island, Mr. Hansard, now a judge of the supreme court of that province, and as a result of that we called a meeting in the city of St. John which was attended by representatives of the three lower provinces. The hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), who was at that time attorney general of the province of Nova Scotia, attended as its representative in the absence of the premier, who was unable to he present in consequence of illness. Others who were present were Messrs. Hansard and Palmer of Prince Edward Island. Mr. Warburton, who had made the motion in the House of Commons. Dr. Daniel, and one or two public men in the province of New Brunswick. We fully discussed and considered the whole question, passed a resolution embodying our views, and then got into correspondence with Sir James Whitney and Sir Lomer Gouin, and asked them to call a meeting of the premiers and representatives of the different provinces, so as to consider this question which was of vital importance to us. That conference was held in Toronto in the autumn of 1910. Among the representatives present were the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Rogers), Sir James Whitney, Sir Lomer Gouin and representatives of all the other Canadian provinces with the exception of British Columbia. I presume that British Columbia did not send a representative to the meeting because it did not feel interested in the question to the same extent that the other provinces did, as under the Act, under which British Columbia came into the union, there is an irreducible number Mr. HA ZEN.
fixed below which representation in British Columbia cannot fall no matter how small the population of the province should become. In other words, British Columbia, which came into the union, after the four original provinces, and before Prince Edward Island became part of the confederation, had inserted in the Act determining the terms of union a provision that under ill circumstances its representation should be fixed at six, and that it should not fall below six; so that if the population of the province should become smaller than it was at the time it entered the union, its representation would still be six members. The conference deliberated in regard to the question very fairly and very candidly.	I do not think that I
am revealing any secret when I say that there was a very general feeling among the members of the conference that something should be done to meet the case of the maritime provinces so far as their representation was concerned. But when my hon. friend puts forward the statement, as he has done to-night, that the representation of no province should fall below that which it had when it entered the union I am afraid that my hon. friend has not given full consideration to the question. That view was put forward at the conference and at once we found ourselves face to face with this condition of affairs. Under the British North America Act the representation of the pivotal province of Quebec was never to be less than 65 in number. Ontario entered the union with 82 members. The people of Quebec have the expectation that at some day, it may be in the near future or it may be farther away, Quebec will be equal in population to Ontario. That hope and ambition may or may not be realized but see what it would mean if it were realized and there was a clause put in this Act to the effect that the popular representation of the provinces should never fall below what it was originally placed at in 1867 or when the provinces entered the union. It would mean that Quebec would have the same or as large a population as Ontario and yet the representation of Quebec would remain at 65, would not increase at all, while the representation of Ontario would not fall below 82. It looked like an insurmountable objection at first, but there was a very strong disposition among the representatives who came from the west, who came from Ontario, and among the members of the conference generally that some exception ought to be made in the case of the maritime provinces. The conference adjourned without taking action as several of the representatives of the different provinces said that they did not feel like committing their provinces to any' course of action on the subject until they had had an opportunity

merits and legislatures. The conference adjourned with the understanding that it would be called together at some future date after the census had been taken and before a redistribution had taken place in order that some decision might be come to along the line of doing something, in so far as the maritime provinces are concerned, in the way of fixing an irreducible minimum for their representation. I may say that, from conversations I have had since with the premiers of different provinces and with gentlemen from different parts of Canada who were present at the conference, I do not at all despair of an agreement being come to between the provinces themselves under which an arrangement will be made that will be eminently satisfactory to those of us who come from the lower provinces.
I fully agree with many of the reasons advanced in support of a contention of that sort. At the time of confederation there were onjy the four provinces. No man in the wildest flights of .fancy, could foresee the greatly changed conditions that were going to come over Canada or anticipate the day when there would be thousands and hundreds of thousands of people flowing into the northwestern country, a country little known at that time and a country that was hardly thought to be fit for settlement. The whole condition and complexion of that country has been changed, and had the men who were delegates to the Quebec conference before 1867 anticipated what was in store they never would have agreed to the terms regarding representation that they did agree to when the conditions were entirely different from what they have become since and when no man anticipated that these greatly- changed conditions would come about in the course of a few years. We find the other provinces being added to from time to time, an empire almost being added to the province of Quebec; we find provinces carved out of what was then just prairie land in the west belonging to the Hudson's Bay Company, first the province of Manitoba, followed by the two great provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, and we find a large addition made to the province of Ontario. But, situated as we are in the lower provinces, hemmed in on both sides either by the sea, by the state of Maine or the province of Quebec, there is no possibility of an extension of territory and we feel that this territory out of which these other provinces in the west have been carved has been purchased with the money of the Canadian taxpayers, with the money of the people of the lower provinces, with the money of the people of every other part of Canada and that the land belonged equally to us as it did to the other parts of Canada.
Under the physical and geographical conditions that prevail, no part of that- do-144
main can come back to us. But we do claim that on account of the tremendous additions made to the west in territory, a share in the burden of purchasing which we cheerfully bore in the general interests of the whole Dominion, and considering that we were among the original provinces of Canada, which made possible the great idea of a united Dominion from ocean to ocean across the northern part of this American continent, we do claim, I say that we are entitled to generous consideration, and especially so in view of the fact that the devolpment of that western country has attracted from our farms, our workshops and our fisheries, so many of our young men, who, had they remained, would have contributed to the wealth and influence of their native province. In view of all these circumstances and the sacrifices we have made, we believe that we should not be put in the humiliating position of having our pride wounded, census after census, by finding that our representation has to be diminished in this House, and that to-day we are not holding nearly as influential a position in the confederacy, so far as to representation in Canada, as we did in its early years. And, while that general statement is true in reference to the lower provinces, there is an even stronger claim on behalf of Prince Edward Island. There is no question to my mind, that history shows that the men who represented Prince Edward Island when the terms of union _ were brought about in 1871, firmly believed that provision had been made for the minimum number of six mem- . bers that would represent that province in this House of Commons. That was at the time a larger number than the population of Prince Edward Island would have warranted, and the representatives of the island distinctly understood and so [DOT]reported to the people what the terms of the arrangement were, that there was an irreducible minimum of six members below which the representation of the island would never fall. The delegates from Prince Edward Island had before them the fact that only the year, before, British Columbia, which then had not as large a population as Prince Edward Island had when it entered the union-secured terms under which it was provided that tire representation of British Columbia should be six members in this House of Commons and that it should never fall below that number. That privilege having been agreed to in the case of British Columbia, it constitutes to my mind a tremendously strong argument in favour of a similar provision being inserted with regard to the representation oif the lower provinces.
I have spoken to-night because I think it is important that this question should be kept before this House and because of the direct personal appeal made to me



by my colleague from the city of St. Joha (Mr. Pugsley). I understand that the next conference of provincial premiers will he held during this coming summer, and that correspondence on the subject is already taking place between the Premier of New Brunswick and the other provincial premiers. I understand that Sir James Whitney and Sir Lomer Gouin, who are recognized as the joint chairmen, are willing to call a meeting to consider the matter, and I have every hope an agreement will be come to under which it can be arranged that the representation of the lower provinces shall not fall below what it is at the present time. And, while I entertain my opinion about our representation as strongly as I ever did, yet I do not believe that the proper means of accomplishing the object we have in view is by opposing the present measure which seeks to put Manitoba on a plane of equality with the other western provinces of Canada. So far as that measure is concerned it is intended as a measure of fair-play to the province of Manitoba. No one who looks at the map of the Dominion of Canada can see the position Manitoba occupies in comparison with Alberta and Saskatchewan, so far as the extent of territory is concerned, wihout feeling that a great injustice was done Manitoba. Every fair-minded man must admit it is only just that its boundaries should be extended, so that it may become comparable in that respect to the newer provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. Every one must feel that this injustice should not be continued longer to the old province of Manitoba, that has blazed the way and opened up to civilization that western country which has now become so potent and important a factor in the public life of Canada. The proposal in this legislation is to redress these grievances, and I do not think any man in this House should object to that. I have heard nothing to lead me to suppose that Manitoba is being treated with anything less than fair and generous justice if this Bill becomes law. I do not believe that we of the maritime provinces have anything to gain by setting our face against this measure which is calculated to do justice to the. western part of this country. Bather, I think we will advance our interests and the case we have at heart- not only in the matter of representation, but in the future as regards the financial terms-by gaining the goodwill and support of our friends in the we3t if we accord this measure generous support. Let us treat Manitoba now in the broad spirit in which we ourselves hope to be dealt with when the question comes before par-Mr. HAZEN.
liament (as it will in the not far distant future) of better times for the maritime provinces. We have the assurance of the right hon. the Prime Minister that the question of compensation to which the maritime provinces are entitled will be dealt with when the question of giving over to the western provinces the control of their public lands is brought for consideration before parliament, and we will not have to wait until the dim and distant future to see that happy day. We have the assurance of my right hon. leader that when that time comes the claims of the maritime provinces will be fairly and reasonably considered, and we may then expect that we will be placed in as good a financial position relatively as the other provinces are. I do not concur with the view expressed by my hon. friends opposite that it is desirable now to hamper the present question with the consideration of that compensation to which we are entitled in the lower provinces, or by an expression of opinion regarding the representation of the maritime provinces as to which I believe this House is practically a unit now, and which I sincerely hope will be dealt with effectively at the meeting of the premiers to be held during the coming summer. If it is not dealt with effectively at that meeting, the question will arise as to what attitude may fairly be taken, having regard to the constitution, for the purpose of redressing the undoubted grievances we labour under. Only a few years ago, in 1891, Nova Scotia had twenty-one members, New Brunswick had sixteen members, and Prince Edward Island had six members, but to-day there has been a great reduction and New Brunswick has only thirteen members, Prince Edward Island four, and Nova Scotia eighteeln. But while my hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley) is now calling for the redress of these grievances, he overlooks the fact that we lost representation under the census of 1901, and that at that time, while he was not a member of this House, he was an influential supporter of the government of the day. How does it come, that he did not then exert his influence with the government, to have existing conditions remedied?
Nothing was done at that time. We sustained the loss of representation. The census of 1911 shows that we shall sustain a still further loss. But I believe that we from the maritime provinces, uniting on both sides of politics in supporting a claim of this kind, can with confidence ^appeal to this House regardless of party 'affiliations, to do what it can to effect a remedy for a state of affairs that so affects our pride, and will affect our status and influence in the future as a part of this confederacy.	*

I am afraid that my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries possesses a greater optimism in regard to the sense of fair-play of the parliament of Canada with regard to this matter than the facts of the case warrant. My hon. friend has not been in this House during the last seven or eight years and listened to the discussions on this question by hon. members from all parts of Canada. I have listened to his very pleasant speech with a great deal of interest; but I want to point out to him that a conference of provincial Premiers alone will not settle this vexed question of the rights of the maritime provinces. It will require a conference participated m, not only by provincial Premiers, but by the Premier of the Dominion and the federal parliament before we can arrive at a conclusion. If my hon. friend will take the trouble to go over the debates and votes to which he has referred, I think he will find that not a man from the west of Lake Superior, and very few west of the maritime provinces, voted for the motion of the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte), or for the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Queens, Prince Edward Island (Mr. McLean). There wjere a few from the province of Ontario; I do not think there was one from the province of Quebec; and the remainder were membeirs f^om the maritime provinces, regardless of politics. Now, my hon. friend has travelled all around the question, and has given, I think, in a fair manner, the arguments pro and con. It is true, he has tried to show that the attitude of the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley), to-night is not consistent with the statements he made in this House two years ago. But, after all, my hon. friend from St. John was fair in stating the facts as they were in 1910, just as he has stated them to-night. My hon. friend from York (Mr. Crocket), was claiming as a matter of right that our representation should not be reduced below the point at which it exists to-day. My hon. friend from St. John was not claiming that as a matter of right, because he said the Privy Council had decided that as a matter of right our representation must be reduced, and, therefore, the only way in which our present representation could be maintained was as a matter of justice^ to us by the remainder of the Dominion. We may just as well face this thing as it is. We may as well admit that as a matter of law, on a proper construction of the British North America Act, as settled once for all by the Privy Council, our representation must go down unless our population increases in equal proportion to that of the province of Quebec. There is no use of beating around the bush and saying that we have any legal right 144}
in the matter, because we have not. Therefore, we come down to the question: Will the rest of Canada give to us as an equitable (right that which we assumed we were safeguarding when we came into the union? I agree with the statement of my hon. friend that if the representatives of the maritime provinces at the Quebec Conference had the faintest idea that our representation would be reduced below what it was as fixed at confederation, they would not have accepted the terms then proposed. But, unfortunately, conditions have changed and our representation has been reduced; and, unfortunately, as the law stands to-day, it will continue to be reduced unless our population increases much more rapidly in the future than it has done in the past. We must have a change in the British North America Act if this reduction is to cease, and how are we going to get that change? My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries says: ' Let this Bill go through; you will only be injuring your case if you raise an objection now, because you will hear from the rest of the people of Canada if you are not friendly towards them.' My experience is that the best time to get anything from another party is when he wants to get something from you. That may be a sordid way of looking at the matter; but my hon. friend will find that if the province of Manitoba gets her boundaries extended and her money grant increased, and if the province of Ontario gets all the rest of the Northwest Territory lying west of Hudson bay, and if the province of Quebec gets all the remainder of the territory lying east of Hudson bay, all of the available land in Canada will have been divided among all the other provinces, and they will have got the financial arrangements that they want, which are grossly unfair to the maritime provinces, he will be reckoning without his host. He will be leaning on a broken reed if he expects that the other provinces, after they have gained all these advantages, are going to turn around and say: You poor people of the maritime provinces have been badly used; we cannot give you more money or land, but we will give you more representation. I want my hon. friend to consider that before he throws his cards on the table. It may be said that I am taking a sordid view of the situation. I think I am taking a common-sense view, and I want my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, as one of the representatives of the maritime provinces in the government, to look the facts in the face. If we have a conference of all the provinces, and have the matter discussed in parliament before Manitoba gets her boundaries extended, and before Ontario gets hers, and before Quebec gets the rest of the territory, and

before they all get improved financial treatment, I think we shall be in a much better position to obtain just treatment for the maritime provinces. Therefore, I think, from the standpoint of the maritime provinces and from the standpoint of common prudence, the members of this House would do well to consider, very carefully, the amendment offered by the hon. member for St. John. I do not know that anything I may say will have any influence with my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries; but I warn him now, and I warn the people of the maritime provinces, that the bait which the leader of this House is holding out to them may be very useless; it may be something that may not be realized for years to come. As I have already pointed out, it is all verv well for the Minister of (Marine and Fisheries to say, I have faith to believe that this will come in a short time. I know perhaps as much about the feeling on this matter as he does, although I am not a member of the government, and, as I read the political horoscope to-day, the possibility of the three western provinces getting their land is very much farther in the future than it has been at any time in the last ten years; and if the maritime provinces are to be compelled to wait until the land is given to those provinces before they get a readjustment of their financial arrangements, I believe they are doomed to great disappointment before the promised land is reached.
What is true in my statement regarding financial matters, is doubly true regarding my statement as to the question of representation. Therefore, Sir, I say again, it behoves the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, who perhaps in one sense ought to be the special representative of the maritime provinces in this case, to look very carefully into this question, and consider it very seriously before he attempts to vote down the amendment proposed by the member for St. John.

Pretty nearly.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Then all I have to say is that I do not quite understand the. statement. In the first place the resolution which has been moved by the hon. member for St. John does not allude Mr. CARVELL.
at all to the question of representation, but to the question of financial terms, and the hon. gentleman desires, according to the terms of his proposed amendment, that nothing should be done in respect to placing Manitoba on a basis of equality with Alberta and Saskatchewan until the Premiers of Canada have been called together and held a conference. Well, I am bound to say that I do not exactly see the significance of that. I am not aware that the Premiers of Canada were called together in conference at the time Saskatchewan and Alberta were constituted.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am not aware that the Premiers of the various provinces of Canada were consulted about the financial terms granted to Alberta and Saskatchewan.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am not aware that at any one'of the many occasions on which individual provinces have had a change for their advantage made in the financial terms which they received from this Dominion, that there has been a conference of the Premiers. The only conference of the Premiers in regard to which any such action was taken, that I can recall, speaking from memory, is the one which has been already alluded to so many times in the course of this debate. Now; the member for St. John says that this measure proposes to ignore all the other provinces. Well, the other provinces are no more ignored now that they were when Alberta and Saskatchewan were constituted. As far as I am aware the moneys proposed to be paid to Alberta and Saskatchewan were to be paid out of the treasury of Canada, and I do not know any other source from which it was proposed to derive them. Therefore, I assume that there should have been just as good reason for consulting the Premiers of the other provinces of Canada then as now, but they were not consulted. No one of the hon. gentlemen who have urged this point with so much insistence had a word to say about calling any conference of the Premiers of the various provinces of Canada at that time. Then I do not exactly understand how the conference of provincial Premiers is to work out this question. Are they to vote by provinces? Are they to vote by the accidental number of representatives who happen to be present from the various provinces? Are they to vote by population, or how are they to vote?
Would it not be fair to have them present at a conference though?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Would it not be fair to have them there?
Yes, if they are not satisfied, would it not be fair and just to have them at a conference?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not know that there is any great advantage in calling the provincial premiers together in a conference unless we are going to pay some attention to their conclusions. If we are to call them together in a conference, then surely we are to be governed to some extent at! least, by their conclusions. Well, suppose the provinces are not unanimous, are we to be governed by the majority, and if so, by what majority? By the majority of population, by the majority of a number of provinces, or by the majority of delegates who happen to be there incidentally to represent any province. That is what I asked the hon. member from St. John.
The Minister of Marine and Fisheries says the provincial premiers are going to be called for some purpose or another.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Oh no, he says they have been called together for the purpose of seeing whether or not the provinces of Canada, other than the maritime provinces, would not all come to an agreement that the representation of the maritime provinces should not be decreased below what it is at the present time, and they failed tq come to any such agreement. Some of the provinces, I understand, were willing, and some were not willing. At all events no agreement was reached. Suppose a similar result obtains in regard to this matter, what conclusion are we to adopt? Every hon. member knows that in the end the final conclusion in respect to any such matter as this must rest upon the responsibility of the federal government and upon no other responsibility, just as it rested in 1905 upon the responsibility of the government that was then in power. We are doing no more to-day, as I have already stated a great many times, for the enlarged province of Manitoba than was done for the adjoining provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan in 1905. However, my hon. friend from St. John has moved his amendment, and it is understood that matters of a controversial nature were not to be finally dealt with tonight. I would be very glad, therefore, to let the clause stand, and see if we can make any progress with some of the other clauses of the Bill, and resume the discussion upon this clause if that course meets with the approval of the committee to-morrow, or when the Bill is next taken into consideration.

I would like to say a word in regard to this matter on behalf of my province, and I must say that I cannot quite grasp the reasoning
of the leader of the House when he wanted to indicate that there was no necessity for a conference, that you would not know what to do with that conference if you did get one. Yet my hon. friend two days ago told us that when he comes to hand back the lands to Manitoba and the other provinces, he is going to call a conference of the provincial governments of Canada to consider
