Mr. MxVCDONALD. My hon. friend from Peterborough generally manages to throw some light upon any problem which he undertakes to discuss, ibut I am bound to say on this occasion he has only succeeded in so clouding up the matter that one hardly knows what he means. Certainly there is going to be some kind of a conference according to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries this year, to consider the question of representation. I would like to know when these gentlemen get together how they are going to be allowed to vote, how their judgment is to find expression. Are they to be allowed to come to any decisions at all, are there any votes to be taken, or what are they going to do?
According to the Prime Minister, you cannot have that kind of a conference because when he has his conference he will not allow anything of that kind. The Prime Minister will see on deliberation, that what the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley), is asking him to do, is to to have a conference before changing the debt allowance of this particular province in order to consult the other provinces on that subject because it is an important one and one on which they have a right to be consulted, and at the same time, he can deal with the question of disposing of the lands if he wants to. The leader of the government says: I am going to give to Manitoba this subsidy and then I will cal] a conference in regard to another matter. The Minister of Finance when he came to deal with that question pleaded with the leader of the opposition that he should try to be a statesman and not a politician, and my hon. friend set the pace for .all the government, in which he was followed by the Minister of the Interior, but he himself was neither a statesman nor a politician, he was a sentimentalist, willing to grant subsidies to pathfinders. That was about the only reason the minister was able to give to the House for this increased debt allowance. Pathfinders should get more money, because they are pathfinders, and a pathfinding province should get more than any other portion of the Dominion. After you have paid off the pathfinders, then we will have a conference to settle that question, after you have disarranged the debt allowance all over Canada and created a disparity and unfairness of treatment of different provinces, we will sit down and talk it over. That seems to be the attitude of the government in this matter.
My hon. friend from Prince Edward Island (Mr. Hughes) put before us the situa-Hr. BURNHAM.
tion of his province. That province has never had any crown lands, it has had no revenue producing assets of any kind, which are common to all the other provinces of the Dominion. Why should not Prince Edward. Island get special treatment in connection with this Bill? It may not be a province peopled with pathfinders, but nevertheless its people are entitled to consideration and consideration now. If we are to have any haste about this thing, if the demand of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Rogers) is so imperious and insistent, that he has to be settled with at once, and all of the other provinces have to wait, Prince Edward Island will have to worry along with $1,028,293.41 a year less than Manitoba. The province from which I have the honour to come, which has 30,000 or 40,000 more population and consequently, more institutions to deal with, will receive under this. Bill $738,884.91 per annum less than Manitoba.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hew .much more does Saskatchewan receive?

My right hon. friend does not want to get away from that proposition and I shall deal with it in a moment. I am saying here, that when the hon. member says to the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) that he would not have a conference until some time in the dim and distant future, that when he called a collection of people together he would not allow them to do anything except to look at him. .In the meantime, the other provinces in the Dominion are being treated in this ungenerous way.
Take New Brunswick. Every year from the passing of this Bill that province will receive $42,794.43 less than the province of Manitoba, which has practically the same population. Then why should British Columbia stand and wait? Is the Minister of Interior more powerful than Dick McBride? Is that the position to-day that he can come here and say we must have all we are asking for and we must have it immediately without consultation with anybody and every other province can go hang in the meantime while British Columbia, which is a province of pathfinders and should therefore commend itself to the Finance Minister, will have to struggle along with $756,323.99 per year less than Manitoba, and some time we will call you to our councils, look at you and state what we are going to do about this thing? That is the position to-day, they are handing out to Manitoba this generous gift covering three years of alleged arrears over and above all this disparity that exists in regard to these im-dividual provinces.
The Prime Minister a moment ago wanted to make a comparison with Saskatchewan. Let us look at the problem of how this sub-

sidy should he dealt with. Manitoba as a province of the Dominion has existed since 1870, it took part in all the conferences held with regard to provincial subsidies and, in the meantime, accepted without ever a quiver or complaint in 1906 and 1907, the amount of money which the federal government had voted in accordance with the resolution passed at the conference. Every one who was in the House at the time or who has looked at the debate knows that while there was an aggressive Conservative party in this House from Manitoba no one alleged that Manitoba required or demanded any special treatment, and the Secretary of State sat still and said nothing. The Minister of the Interior yesterday tried to make us believe that the particular claim of his province at that time received special recognition at the hands of the conference. There is not a single line in the whole renort to be found in the Sessional Papers that warrants that statement. On the contrary the Premier of Ontario and his colleagues went on record in the strongest possible way in declaring that for "the future there should be no special grant of subsidies such as this government proposed to make to Manitoba at this time. Is this confederation a partnership of the different provinces of Canada or is it not? That is the proposition that is at the basis of this whole legislation. One would think to hear these gentlemen talk about these matters that the history of Canada is about written and that our future was not a matter to be considered at all. The only way in which such questions as the extension of boundaries can be fairly solved is the way in which the fathers of confederation did it, when they sat in council at Charlottetown and Quebec and considered the relative positions of each province, what the debt allowance should be and what considerations were peculiar to each province and then attempted to settle the matter fairly. That is what they did in 1906-7, and when under the late government the proportionate amounts to be paid to each province were reconsidered they all met here and dealt with the matter. When my hon. friends come to pick out one province which was to enter confederation after 1867, and to deal with it,_ they did not attempt to defend the proposition except to say that they were dealing with the matter on a basis of federal readjustment. They come along and say, oh this is a province of pathfinders. The same thing was done when the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan were originated, and now they say that for that and no other reasons you must increase the debt allowance, and maue these extra grants to the province of Manitoba. When 'this question of subsidies was before the House of Commons in 1906-7 the financial critic of the opposition who is now the
Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) told the House how these things should be dealt with. I ventured to ask the Minister of Finance on the first, reading of this Bill whether he had looked at this question from that standpoint, and he told us he was not responsible for the individual views of his colleagues. I think my hon. friend the new Minister of Finance could have gone to school to the Minister of Trade and Commerce in regard to these questions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend asked me what was the debt of Manitoba tc-day. There is no assumption by the Dominion of the debt of Manitoba to-day, and therefore it does not enter into the consideration of this question.
Unfortunately for my hon. friend, the Minister of Trade and Commerce did, in 1906-7, lay that down as one of the essential things that should be taken into consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: 1 am satisfied that he did not intend it in that sense at all, because it is not relevant unless the Dominion assumes the debt.

I invite me hon. friend to turn up ' Hansard ' of that year where he will find what the Minister of Trade and Commerce said upon that question. He discussed very fully the resolutions which were then brought before the House by the then Minister of Finance, asking that the resolutions which had been agreed upon by the provinces should be adopted by the House. The present Minister of Trade and Commerce laid down a great many rules which should be followed, and I will take them up. First he said that before the federal government dealt with this question of subsidies they should consider what are the available sources of revenue of a province, they should examine into the expenditure of the province, and find whether it had been wise and prudent, or whether it was one which was likely to lead to a debt so vast that the province would be compelled to come back to the federal parliament and ask for assistance. If their means of revenue were limited, that also should be taken into consideration. Then there was another consideration: Is this to be the last time of asking? he said:	Is the proposition to be
a final one? There has been no suggestion in regard to that subject in this case, and that is a subject upon which we ought to know something before this Bill goes i ut of committee. Hon. gentlemen say that this is the last time Manitoba is coming back. Are we making a full settlement of all financial demands, or will Manitoba be coming back next year? These are things which the Minister of Trade and

Commerce said should be considered. Then he asked: Is it a permanent arrangement? Every Finance Minister, he said, should be careful to see whether it was a permanent arrangement or not. There is nothing here to show that this is a permanent arrangement; on the contrary, we are told that this is not a permanent arrangement. In a year or so we are going to give the lands back to the western provinces, and to make a new deal in which the Minister of the Interior will endeavour to walk off with the larger share of the swag. The result will be that this whole subsidy question wall be reopened. Is there any check put on the debt creating power of the province? was a pertinent question asked by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Is there any check, or is the door left open so that every provincial Premier who wants to be extravagant can come back and make another raid? All this language in regard to the debt will be found in the speech of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, pages 5314 to 5319 in ' Hansard ' of March 25, 1907.	All
these considerations were suggested by him as being absolutely necessary before you could determine what was fair and right in dealing with any province of the Dominion. Then he declared that having a fixed sum you could never have finality, and where you fixed a definite amount you could never have finality, and no payment should be made, except it was made on the percentage basis, or you could never have a final settlement as to the rate of payment which is to be applied to every province. All these considerations the Minister of Trade and Commerce declared to be essential in 1907; and not one of them has been observed by this government; there is no pretence, they are all thrown to the winds. There is only one defence -Saskatchewan and Alberta got so much in 1905, and therefore we have got to give to Manitoba that amount to-day. Now, on what possible ground can this proposition be justified ? What reason can there be for doing that any more than if you were to say to Ontario to-day, vdiich was one of the original partners of confederation, that because her boundaries are being extended to the Hudson bay, you must give her an additional amount. The principal theory upon which the provinces are to be assisted with provincial subsidies is that larger responsibilities are assumed along with the rights accorded to them under the British North America Act. Certain duties were assigned to each provincial legislature to carry out. They were compelled to look after certain services, and we were compelled to look after certain others. The amount of money that was to be expended necessarily by any province depended upon population and Mr. MACDONALD,
like considerations. Now, because, _ forsooth, you are adding to the territory of the province of Manitoba a certaiin area, you say to them: We are going to give you this vast sum of money beginning in 1908,though you had no territory and therefore had no responsibility, and therefore nothing to expend any money for. Manitoba never lost a dollar since 1908 by reason of not having this money, because she never had the territory to spend it on. If the reason for granting this increased subsidy is because you are going to increase the territory of Manitoba, then you have no reason for giving these arrearages, because Manitoba was not spending any money. In 1905 you started out the two new provinces, and from that moment their expenditure began. Along with the rights that were accorded to the provinces under the British North America Act, was a duty imposed upon the legislatures of those provinces, and they had to spend their money. Manitoba has been doing this since 1871 in a limited way, but not a single dollar has she spent since 1908 in addition to what she was spending before, for the reason that she had no more territory on which to spend it. The Minister will search the records of his department in vain previous to confederation down to the present time to find any justification for such a proposition. What are they to be compensated for ? If they had the lands, then they would have been expending some additional amounts upon them, because responsibility begins with the acquisition of the lands. It is purely a sentimental arrangement in order that the Minister of the Interior may go back to Manitoba and tell them: See what I have got out of the Dominion treasury for you, although I had no right to get it.
Are there no damages?

My hon. friend (Mr. Burnham) is a lawyer, I understand, and damages in regard to breach of rights in a legal sense can be assessed upon certain principles. If it were possible to convince my hon. friend, I could easily convince him that these theoretical damages of which he speaks were never found within the purview of any legal considerations nor of any political one, either, up to date.
Two million dollars paid to Manitoba because they did not get the boundaries settled three years ago. Why did they not get their boundaries? It was their own fault. They never said they would take the boundaries until last spring when they took the very limits that the late government offered to them, Yet, the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. White), subsidizing the pathfinders, is going to give them $2,000,000 for nothing. What is going to happen, after they do get the

lands, to the 690 white people up there? The Manitoba government has never spent a five cent piece in actual money in looking after these 690 people or the territory in which they live since 1908, or at any time up to date. The Dominion government looked after that territory and had everything to do with it. The Indians were looked after by the Indian Department, and whatever police work was done was done by the mounted police. If Manitoba gets control of that territory the mounted police will go on looking after the territory at the expense of the Dominion of Canada. This additional bonus which they will receive we have not yet heard mentioned. The result is, that leaving out of consideration altogether the amount which is supposed to be their due for damages for a wrong that was never inflicted, this - Dominion is giving to Manitoba a still further sum of $747.83 every year for every man, woman and child to be found in the added territory. Is it any wonder that my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley), wants to have a conference of the other provinces of the Dominion? When you get down to the real situation in reference to this matter you will find that the Dominion government hands over to this province $747.83 every year for every man, woman and child as a gift to assist in governing the people who are to be found in the added territory in order that Manitoba may be on an equality with Alberta and Saskatchewan. That is the reason that is given.
My hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Rogers), sang a dismal song that the late Premier would not give them what they wanted because they were Conservatives. He was smiling in his cheek when he made that (Statement in this House. It has become an old story how he and the Premier of the province oi Manitoba have been making a football of this question for the last ten years. The Minister of the Interior knows very well that the Manitoba government were preaching that Laurier would not give them a fair deal. They did not want a fair deal. They were sparring for wind and lor time, looking for a grievance, and it is on account of thisi old grievance of theirs that they were feeling so badly, but have succeeded in inducing the new Minister of Finance to give them this $2,000,000 as a present, and a solatium for their wounded feelings. Then my hon. friend was so sorrowful over the fact that this leader of the opposition, when he was Premier, would not give them the swamp lands just when they wanted them. But he said the Canadian Northern could get lands just when they wanted them in Saskatchewan. My hon. friend was worrying tremendously about the Canadian Northern railway. Everybody
who knows anything about Manitoba politics knows that my hon. friend and the Canadian Northern have been cheek by jowl for the last ten years, standing and working together whether it was in regard to swamp lands or any other kind of lands. The Minister of the Interior was certainly drawing a long bow when he attempted to persuade this House that the claim of Manitoba in regard to this debt allowance and increased subsidies was approved by the conference. The contrary is the case as has been proved by my hon. friend from St. John. There is no evidence on the records to justify the statement of the Minister of the Interior. On the contrary, I want to reiterate to my hon. friend who was not at the conference at all, that the Premier and the Attorney General of the province who were there signed and supported the resolution which was presented to them under which they accepted the allowance that they have been receiving from that day down to the present time and never made any kind of a kick, never made any kind of objection as to these side claims. Look what Premier McBride did in regard to British Columbia. He presented his claims and advocated them very seriously. He could not get the representatives of the other provinces to agree with him and he said: I will not join you at all upon this question; you may go and see the Prime Minister if you like, but as far as I am concerned, I will leave the conference and do what I can to secure favourable action upon my demand. The colleagues of the Minister of the Interior, Mr. Roblin and Mr. Campbell, quietly and humbly sat down along with the other Premiers, and representatives of the other provinces and never said a word about these claims, except that they had presented them to the Premier. When these gentlemen would not agree with them that it was right that they should get these extra claims, they said: We are not going to go like Premier McBride, and kick over the traces, or do anything; we will take what we can get in the meantime, and as long as you do not agree with McBride we will go with you. They did so; there was no refusal on their part, as there was on the part of Mr. McBride. If the minister's colleagues, Messrs. Roblin and Campbell, had done what McBride had done in 1906, it would have been open to him to argue that they had a grievance that ought to be remedied, but he comes in and proposes to take the money of the various provinces because Laurier would not give them the boundaries. Since 1908 anybody who went to Manitoba would hear nothing discussed ir. provincial politics, but the declaration of members of the provincial government that this wicked man who had been leading the government of Canada would not

give them fair-play, and would not give them the boundaries. A great many people believed it, who did not know that there was incorporated in the records of this House, a resolution passed in 1908 giving them exactly what they get this year and what they would not take and what no one could possibly induce them to take. These gentlemen did not want to take that until they had the elections over in Manitoba last year. The complaint would have been done away with, if they had accepted these boundaries before the provincial elections were over. These gentlemen wanted a grievance. Mr. Richard McBride asserted, thisi claim for an extra allowance but, finding that his colleagues from the other provinces would not join with him, he would not have anything to do with them and went out and asserted he was right in this matter. These gentlemen did not do anything of the kind; they took the money went home, and now they have succeeded in inducing the government of this country to give them $2,000,000 for absolutely nothing. You say that this is not a finality that this does not close the books, that you are making a deal about lands and about territory, that you are taking from these people the swamp lands, that you are going to make a new arrangement at some time in the future and that when you make that new arrangement about the lands, you will hold a conference. We come to you and say:	Do you think that it is a good
time now to hold a conference because you are dealing with financial arrangements on a certain basis, with an old province of the Dominion, that joined with us three years ago, as a member of the conference that then took place, and where we were told what our course was going to be in the future and what we ought to receive-do you think that it is a fair proposition that you should hold a conference now before you adopt this new arrangement with this one province? That is the proposition of my hon. friend from St. John, it is a reasonable one, and I fail to see upon what ground it can be answered.
The circumstances of this case are such that my hon. friends opposite cannot answer their responsibility to the other provinces of the Dominion by saying they are going to level this up by the two prairie provinces. For the reasons I have given I support the resolution of my hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley). The Minister of Marine and Fisheries rather suggested that my hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley) was not as enthusiastic about the matter of representation as he was at one time, but I can tell the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries) that that idea is purely a figment of his imagination. The maritime provinces were not aroused on this question of represen-Mr. MACDONALD.
tation until after 1901, and the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) was the first to raise the question. He initiated the legal proceedings which were taken to have the question considered before the Supreme Court and the Privy Council and I had the honour of being associated with him, representing the province of Nova Scotia in that argument No man could have presented a stronger case than the hon. member for St. John did before the Supreme Court of Canada, and I want to say that the decision upon that matter was based upon a strict legal interpretation and not upon the consideration of these constitutional rights which ought to have been taken into consideration in arriving at a decision upon such a question. The Supreme Court of Canada, when it has to deal with a question of constitutional rights such as that of representation, will not look at the historical documents which show thd understanding that existed at the time of union, nor at the date which is open to every one and which discloses the intention of the original parties to the compact. The courts never looked at these facts, but decided the question from a technically legal standpoint. However, the right which is claimed now is one which can only be granted as the result of the consent of the various provinces of this Dominion. And, this would be an appropriate time to have this conference, a conference of value, a conference such as the Premier proposes to call with regard to the disposal of the land. Why not have that conference this year? Next year we will have redistribution and if parliament goes on redistributing without an amendment *o the Act of the Imperial parliament to warrant their doing justice to the maritime provinces, the time will be too late and the right which the Minister of Marine and Fisheries says we should obtain, we cannot obtain. I come from ihe province of Nova Scotia, which is discriminated against as a result of this bargain. I come from a province which was one of the first partners of confederation, and has more right to consideration at the hands of this government than lias that eldest of the prairie provinces, great as she is. And, I say that every year 'hereafter until justice is done us, we will be discriminated against, as compared with Manitoba, to the amount of $750,000 a year, I claim that the resolution moved by my hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley) demands the attention of the government, and I am surprised that the Prime Minister coming, as he does, from my own province, and knowing the conditions there, should absolutely submit himself to the dictation of the Minister of the Interior, who, in

this case has succeeded in getting him to do something which is unfair to the other provinces of the Dominion. If Manitoba is entitled to this concession, then let the other provinces of the Dominion be treated fairly at the same time. For my part I say: let Manitoba have every right to which she is entitled as a member of the confederacy, but do not let Manitoba have that which the government refuses to give to Nova Scotia, to New Brunswick, to Prince Edward Island and to the other provinces of the Dominion.

I understood the Prime Minister to say that as the amendment offered by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) was contentious, it would stand over until a future occasion. I have an amendment to move to section 4, and as no doubt that amendment will be contentious also, I want it to be understood that if this amendment is left over we are not to be precluded from moving further amendments.
What is the hon. gentleman's amendment?

When the present amendment is disposed of, I intend to move that subsection 2 of section 4 be stricken out, and the following substituted therefor:
The first half yearly payment under this section shall be made on the first day of July, 1912.

I also give notice that I shall move as an amendment:
That the following clause be inserted in Bill 115 ,as clause 8, immediately following clause 7.
Nothing in this Act shall in any way prejudice or affect the rights that miay actually be enjoyed by the population of that part of the Northwest Territories now added to Manitoba.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
1 wish to say a few words by way of enlightenment to the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) who has undertaken to discuss a question that he apparently knows very little about. I am surprised at some of the statements the hon. gentleman has undertaken to make in this House, for I would expect that in undertaking to discuss an important question such as the one before us, he would have informed himself to some extent so as to be in a position to discuss it intelligently. In the first place, the hon. member (Mr. Macdonald) has asked: why did not Manitoba take her lands when they were offered to her three years ago. Well, I want to tell the hon. gentleman that we have never been offered the lands, neither three years ago, nor at any other time during the reign of the late Liberal government. Such a thing was never offered to us; we pleaded for that as representing Manitoba
time and again, but we never could get that concession from the Liberal government.
What about the resolution of 1908?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The resolution of 1908 did not promise or offer to the province of Manitoba one single solitary acre of land.
You are confusing that with boundaries.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Then my hon. friend (Mr. Macdonald) goes on and undertakes to tell the House that the territory of Keewatin to be added, has never cost the province of Manitoba a solitary dollar. Let me read for his information a few words from a speech delivered by his honoured leader in this House on May 9, 1905. Sir Wilfrid Laurier made the following statement:
No, there is no need for a legislature, because there is no population in Keewatin. Keewatin has been administered for thirty years by the province of Manitoba.
Since 1905 who has administered it? The province of Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The province of Manitoba was administering the district of Keewatin for thirty years, and an attempt was made by the government which my hon. friend supported in 1905 to take it away from us.
Is it or is it not true that although it may have been administered by Manitoba, any expenses connected with the administration of Keewatin were borne by the Federal government?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Certain expenses were borne by the Dominion government. The Lieutenant Governor of the province of Manitoba received $1,000 a year for thirty years as the governor and administrator of the district of Keewatin, but every justice of the peace and magistrate in the province of Manitoba, who received his pay from that province, was a justice of the peace with full power and authority for the administration of 'law and order in the district of Keewatin for thirty years.
Did these justices of the peace receive any salary from the Dominion government?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Justices of the peace, police magistrates, and so on, always received salaries from the province of Manitoba.
Did they receive any extra salary for administering justice with respect to persons charged with crime in the Keewatin territory?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No doubt, in fixing their salaries, due consideration was given to the amount of work they had to do in ad-

ministering that great territory during that length of time. The hon. member for Pictou says we are apparently in great haste in endeavouring to settle this question, and that we should delay it further in order to have a conference. I do not think the facts will bear out the statement of the hon. member for Pictou that either I or any other member of this government, or the government as a whole, are evincing any great haste in the settlement of this question. It has been a very live issue in the province of Manitoba for ten long years. We have been appealing to the government of our predecessors during all that period, and we have not met with much success.
Has the Manitoba government pressed the federal government to give the lands?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We pressed the government of our predecessors to give us equality either with the provinces to the east or the province's to the west. The real grievance of Manitoba rested upon that point. Manitoba claimed that her position was one of inequality with any other province in the Dominion, by reason of the fact that, before the province of Al*-berta and Saskatchewan were formed, she was the only province that was not in possession of her public domain and her national resources. She complained for many years, and received from this parliament, on various occasions during that period, a readjustment of her claims. When the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan were formed in 1905, the province of Manitoba made a special appeal to the gov eminent of the day to be placed in a posi tion of equality either with the provinces to the west or to the east. The older provinces of Canada had their lands and their mines and their minerals, and the provinces of the west then being created were being placed in a much more favourable position than the province of Manitoba. We were told by the right hon. gentleman who was leading the government at thal time that he could not consider at all the question of granting us our lands. Manitoba then undertook to urge its claims on the ground that it was entitled to be placed in a position of equality with the sister provinces to the west. The province of Manitoba presented its claim at the conference, and had it supported by the conference, to be given the same terms and conditions as those given to the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta. The province of Manitoba has not asked this government up to the present time to give them their lands, because they felt that they had established their case at the conference to the satisfaction of every government in this Dominion, and were en-Mr. ROGERS.
titled to the same terms and conditions as the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. Now, the hon. member for St. John says that the Sessional Papers do not establish that Manitoba had made the claims which she did make before that conference. If the hon. gentleman will turn to page 3 in the Sessional Returns, he will find it stated that the return published there consists simply of extracts from what took place at that conference. Therefore the Sessional Papers show on the face of them that it is not a full report of that conference.

Will my hon. friend allow me, because there is an issue between us? iM.y hon. friend made the statement that the records show that the conference had approved of these special claims which the province of Manitoba was making. Now I have no recollection of it. I have searched' the records, and I can find no trace of such a thing. Would my hon. friend be good enough to point out, where it appears that the conference approved of these things?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In answer to my hon. friend, let me say that I told the House yesterday that when Manitoba was invited to be present at that conference, its representatives replied they would only attend upon a certain understanding. They came here with that understanding, and when they arrived, Mr. Roblin presented his case to the conference and a sub-committee was appointed to consider that case, not as my hon. friend from Pictou, I think it was told us, that they were appointed to consider the case of the representatives from British Columbia. In order that I may make it clear to the House, I will read the statement appearing in the official record, as made at that time, by the right hon. gentleman who now leads the opposition, so that you will see that the case of Manitoba and of British Columbia were both dealt with in an entirely different form and in an entirely different way. When British Columbia came here the claim that she had in effect was this: That British Columbia would not be satisfied with the terms and conditions for which that conference was -specifically called to deal with. That conference, as has been stated by the member for St. John, was called to carry out, or to approve, a resolution as passed by a conference held in the province of Quebec in the year 1902. That conference in 1902 laid down that the time had arrived when this government should give to the different provinces of Canada additional subsidies in regard to legislation and to the cost of government, as well as in regard to the changed conditions by the payment of 80 cents per head. The conference was called

to deal with these two specific points, and these two points alone. Manitoba at first refused to attend in case her position would be misunderstood for these points were the only two to be dealt with in that way. British Columbia refused to take part in that conference and Mr. McBride left the meeting because he could not get an additional increase under those two items. Those two items are to-day entirely satisfactory to the province of Manitoba. However, that was the point which Mr. McBride raised in -so far as the province of British Columbia is concerned. Now, here is what Sir Wilfrid Laurier had to say in addressing the joint conference upon that matter:
I have given careful consideration to the memorial of British Columbia's government, and particularly to the request that a commission he appointed for the purpose of inquiring into the financial relations between the Dominion and the province. I have been unable to reach the conclusion that the appointment of such a commission would he the best way of dealing with a question of this kind. I fear that such a course would not lead to the harmonious settlement of the grants to -provinces which all should desi-re to bring about. However, I regard the matter at present more as one for the opinion of the conference than for the judgment of the Dominion government. You have assembled for the purpose of considering -the sums which should properly he paid by the Dominion to the provinces in the way of subsidies and allowance for the maintenance of government. The British Columbia proposal comes entirely within the chief purpose of this conference. If _ this conference, after hearing -Mr. McBride's arguments in support of this contention, reach the conclusion that an arbitration should take place, through a commission, foi the purpose of _ dealing with the claim of British Columbia, that would present the matter to the Dominion government in a new light, and while I am not prepared to express any final opinion, I can say at once that such -a recommendation from the conference would have great weight with us, and we should feel bound to give it further consideration. While I give you this expression of my own views and of the views of mv colleagues who are here with me, I shall, if you will permit me, offer a suggestion. I think there is a disposition on the part of the conference to recognize that the conditions in British Columbia, owing to the vastness of her territory, to its mountainous character, and the s-parseness of her population, create exceptional difficulties which should be taken into consideration in the adjustment of the distribution of the grants in aid of provincial governments. I am mvseilf disposed to admit that such is the case, I would stronglv advise that Mr. McBride avail himself of the good disposition which is manifested in the conference -and at once approach the question of that allowance, in adid+ion to that already contemplated, should be made to meet British Columbia's difficulties. It is a question which after all can better be settled here than anvrt-here else. I feel assured that the conference will be willing to deal with the matter in a spirit of fairness to British Columbia I pro pose therefore that we shall leave you to discuss the question frankly with one another and co-me to you again when probably you will have reached some satisfactory agreement.
Now that was where British Columbia came in in connection with the other provinces. Manitoba took no exception to the proposal as made by the conference held at Quebec in 1892, and when her representatives attended that conference at that time, they were careful then, as in 1906, to have a note made on the records of that date, that the case of Manitoba should receive special consideration, and at the foot of the report of that conference of 1902 you will find the note:
The following -paragraph was added in the
case of -Manitoba :
It is, however, to be distinctly understood that in asking for this conference on the basis set forth,^ it shall in no way prejudice Manitoba's claims upon the Dominion in respect to her lands.
and so forth.
Now, Mr. Chairman, that is the position -which Manitoba has -taken all along in respect to this matter, and her representatives attended the conference in 1906 with the distinct understanding that her claims against the Dominion were not to be prejudiced by the fact of their attendance there, and by Manitoba's acceptance of the terms in respect of the government and legislative allowance, as well as the allowance in connection with the 80 cents per head. I read to this House yesterday, and I am not going to detain hon. gentlemen by reading it again to-night, that when that conference took place, a subcommittee was appointed and appointed specifically to give consideration to this matter. On that occasion the hon. member for St. John, because I heard my colleagues talking abo-ut it at the time, was very good and very generous in supporting or giving consideration to that particular matter, and when the resolution embodying the arrangement agreed to by that conference-not only by the subcommittee, but by all members of the conference-Mr. Roblin who was presenting the matter moved this resolution, as reported in the Toronto ' Globe,' which published a full report of the official minutes of the meeting taking place at that time:
Moved by Mr. Roblin, seconded by Mr. Peters, that the report of the committee charged with the preparation of the resolutions embodying tbe views of the conference on the resolutions of 1902 be adopted, and it was unanimously adopted as follows:
Whereas the members of this conference are of the opinion that it is desirable in the interests of the people of Canada and essential to the development of the provinces

that an immediate provision he made for an increase of the subsidies granted by the Dominion to the several provinces and for the award to the provincial governments' by Canada of an amount sufficient to meet the costs of the administration of criminal justice not exceeding twenty cents per head of the population; therefore it is unanimously resolved (1) that the subject matter of -the resolutions adopted by the conference of the representatives of the several provinces held at Quebec in December, 1902, and which were shortly thereafter presented to the government of the Dominion and which were ratified bv the legislature of the then existing provinces, except that of British Columbia, he now pressed upon the government of the Dominion for immediate and favourable action, under reserve of the right of a.ny province to now submit-
To now submit.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: To now submit to such government, memoranda in writing concerning any claims it may have to larger sums than those set out in the said resolutions, or to additional consideration for recognition.
For recognition.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I want to tell my hon. friend from St. John, that Manitoba placed her claim in the hands of the Dominion government then and there, in writing. I want to tell him furthermore, that no other province in this Dominion from that day to this, as far as I know, has placed any claim in the hands of the government in writing in respect to the said matter.

The records show that immediately following the adoption of that resolution, British Columbia submitted her claim, and it was dealt with by the conference, including the representatives from Manitoba, and it was rejected, the conference passing a unanimous resolution which the representatives of Manitoba also assented to, declaring against arbitration but recommending that British Columbia receive a reasonable additional allowance for civil government of $100,000 a year for ten years.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend does not appear to have understood what I mentioned a minute ago, that British Columbia's claim was a special one which simply dealt with the two specific items which the conference was called to consider-that of the subsidies for government and legislation, and the matter of 80 cents per head, as stated by the then Premier himself, whose remarks I quoted a few minutes ago.
Outside of that no other province made any claim under the reservation as provided by these resolutions that they should make appeal to the government for additional consideration under the reserve so Mr. ROGERS.
stated. Manitoba has been the only province that came under that particular clause from that day to this.
Have we heard now from my hon. friend all that he relies on as showing that the conference approved of the special claims of Manitoba or is there anything else that will tend to prove it?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think I have told the hon. gentleman all that is necessary to inform him to-night. If to-morrow he wants more information I will, if possible, suppiy him with it.
There is not a word to show thait the conference approved of it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I told my hon. friend that our claim was presented at that conference and it was only after the conference gave it full and fair consideration that they were willing and did vote unanimously in order that this reservation should he placed in the resolution.
That does not approve of it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is a statement that should1 be plain enough in respect to the matter and should satisfy the hon.. gentleman if he wants to be satisfied, in regard to the position. My hon. friend has moved an amendment to the effect that we should submit this matter to a further conference. This course is adopted in pursuance of the same policy which has been pursued by the- hon. gentlemen opposite for the past fourteen years. They have attempted to find one cause after another to stir up one province against another, in order that Manitoba might be prevented from occupying a position of equality with the other provinces of Canada.

Was the minister or any other member of the government of Manitoba aware of the terms of the .address passed by the parliament of Canada in 1907 asking for certain imperial legislation to ratify the new provincial subsidies in which the terms were used that this settlement was to be final and conclusive? Did anybody oppose this legislation in the Imperial parliament on behalf of the government of Manitoba as it was opposed on behalf of British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If my hon. friend will read the Act I think he will find it is there under subsection 7. That clause was put in order to cover the very resolution which I have been reading to this House which wa3 passed unanimously at the request of Manitoba, and in order that Manitoba's claims should be protected and it is incorporated in the Act to which my hon. friend refers.
That clearly refers to British Columbia.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: Would the amounts paid into the treasury be customs duties?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Customs and excise.
Is not the great city of Winnipeg the wholesale distributing point of the whole of the west?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Toronto is too.
Would it be fair to take the figures of the great city of Montreal and attribute them to the province of Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Now, I ask you if Manitoba, from that point of view if from no other, has not a good case to present to this House to have her position rectified, and to be placed on a footing of equality with the other provinces. That is all Manitoba has ever asked, that is all they are asking by this Bill. The hon. gentleman says that we should have a conference to consider the question of representation in the maritime provinces.
Those figures that the hon. gentleman has presented of money paid into the various provinces, are they based on the customs?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Based on customs and excise. I want to say that I sympathize with the hon. member for St. John and the other members from the maritime provinces in the claim they make in regard to representation. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries has dealt fully with the conference that was held here in 1910. I had the pleasure of attending that conference, and the question which the hon. gentleman refers to was given careful consideration. The great majority of the members of that conference considered that it would be in the interest of this Dominion if most careful consideration were given to the representa-

tions then made. I think that one or two gentlemen present at that conference were not disposed to give sympathetic consideration to the proposals made by the maritime provinces. HoweveT, my feelings in regard to the matter have not changed, and I am sure that I represent the feelings of the people of western Canada. I am satisfied they are willing at all times to join any conference, and to give the most liberal interpretation to any propositions that may be made by representatives from the maritime provinces with a view to secure a remedy for the grievance of which they complain. I presume another conference will be held before very long, and when this question comes up, I am satisfied that the representatives from western Canada will be prepared to give a sympathetic and generous support to the claims of the maritime provinces. With regard to the amendment of the hon. member for St. John, I think the object is to delay as long as possible a settlement of this vexed question relating to the province of Manitoba. But I can assure him that no matter how many amendments he may move, we will be able to carry through this House the Bill which is now before us, and in so doing we will be rectifying an injustice from which Manitoba has been suffering for a long period.

By this amendment I trust the committee will realize that we do not ask for any delay that would be prejudicial to Manitoba. The first payment of the subsidy could only be made next July. Now, in the amendment we name the exact figures suggested by the Minister of Finance. All that we propose to attain by this amendment is that the Governor in Council shall have authority to pay to the province of Manitoba an amount not exceeding the figures which are named here. But before doing that a conference of the Premiers of the different provinces should be called to consider this matter, and also to consider what it would be equitable and just to allow in respect of the debt account to the other provinces of Canada by reason of this increase in the debt allowance to Manitoba. There need be no delay. We do not limit the Governor in Council at all, all we ask is that before deciding this matter, before disturbing the financial position of Manitoba, which necessarily does an injustice to the other provinces until they are likewise considered, we ask that a conference of the Premiers of the provinces should take place with the Federal government, to consider this matter vejy fully. Now, the Minister of the Interior gave me several surprises. I am surprised that he does not consent to the reasonable and fair proposition I have made. It looks as if he Wished to rush this thing through and disturb the financial relations between the different provinces. He thinks if he gets Mr. ROGERS.
this Bill once on the statute-book, then, when the conference takes place, he will be just that much ahead in the game. I think this is a pretty tough business on the other provinces of Canada, and I hope my hon. friend will not persist in a course so unreasonable and so unfair as he now threatens to take.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I will make a proposition to the committee. I understand that the clause under consideration is not to be disposed of this evening, as it is a contentious clause, nor will the amendment be disposed of this evening. I propose that the committee go through the other clauses of the Bill to which there is no objection, and then we will rise. In that way we will make some progress at this sitting.

There will be some discussion upon the clause relating to swamp lands, but as to the unimportant clauses it would not take five minutes to put them through. But we shall run against a snag almost immediately when we strike the swamp lands. There are a good many on this side of the House who think that is the most indefensible thing in the world, to take away from this province these swamp lands and then hold out the idea that in a year or two we are going to give them all back again.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I have no idea of arguing the objection that my hon. friend takes, I was merely endeavouring to ascertain, in order that we should make some progress, what clauses are objectionable. These we can reserve, pass the others, report progress, and rise if we are not going to dispose of the Bill finally this evening.
If we disposed of the contentious clauses the non-contentious clauses would not take five minutes, so that there would be nothing gained.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Let us take five minutes to the non-contentious clauses.
From the costume of many hon. members I conclude that there must be some pleasant function going on here and, therefore, I think we had better rise.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
